title: October 2026 good for PV Production in Europe, but South of France and Ukraine missout - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
In a new weekly update for pv magazine,
, a DNV company, reports that solar irradiance across much of Europe was around 10% above average in October 2026, reaching up to 25% above average in central Europe and the Baltic States due to persistent high-pressure systems.
However, southern France and the Black Sea region experienced below-average irradiance due to cloud cover and storms, while severe winds caused widespread power outages across western Europe.
06 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
Irradiance was above average across much of Europe in October 2026, as extended periods of high pressure produced clearer skies and offset several cloudy and unsettled intervals. Conditions were particularly favourable across central Europe and the Baltic States. However, low-pressure systems reduced irradiance in southern France and around the Black Sea, while several damaging autumn storms crossed western Europe, according
to analysis using the
Solcast API
Monthly irradiance was around 10% above the October average across large parts of the continent. The strongest positive anomalies occurred in Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary, where irradiance reached as much as 25% above average. Similarly large percentage increases were recorded in the Baltic States, although shorter daylight hours at these northern latitudes limited average daily irradiance to around 1.3 kWh/m².
Recurring high-pressure systems suppressed cloud formation and produced more settled, sunnier conditions across much of Europe. This pattern was consistent with a positive phase of the North Atlantic Oscillation during September and October, which strengthens the Azores high over the Atlantic, with increased high pressure ridging across Western Europe.
Not all regions fared so well. Irradiance across the southern half of France finished around 5% below average. Ukraine and Moldova were as much as 10% below average. Repeated low-pressure systems and weather fronts brought greater cloud cover and rainfall to the Black Sea area, limiting the amount of sunlight reaching the surface.
Southern France’s irradiance deficit was the result of an accumulation of several factors. Storm Adam in mid-October produced intense rainfall and flash flooding across parts of France, Spain and Corsica. Southern France was also subject to additional “épisode cévenol” thunderstorm events occurred during the month. These are a regional phenomenon which develops when warm, moisture-laden Mediterranean air encounters colder air near the elevated terrain of southern France, generating deep cloud and heavy rainfall that can sharply reduce irradiance.
Lower GHI across southern France and surrounding areas reflects the extensive cloud associated with the storm.
Two further named storms affected western Europe during the second half of October. Storm Austin crossed southern England and France, bringing wind and rain, while Storm Boelo later struck Scotland and Northern Ireland with severe gusts of over 130 km/h. The associated cloud and rainfall disrupted otherwise favourable irradiance conditions, while the strong winds damaged electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure. Power outages affected nearly 300,000 customers in France during Storm Austin, while cuts affecting 800,000 people were reported following Storm Boelo.
The Severe Weather Index uses Numerical Weather Prediction data to represent winds associated with larger weather systems and thunderstorms, with higher values indicating more severe conditions.
Elevated values extended from the Atlantic across the United Kingdom and into the North Sea. When forecast in advance, such conditions may prompt operators to prepare for potential grid interruptions, with actions such as pre-emptive charging of batteries.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

title: Türkiye targets 175 GW of solar, wind capacity by 2040 - pv magazine Global
政策分类路径: 政策 > 战略规划型政策 > 规划目标
政策分类依据: 土耳其2040国家能源愿景提出175GW风光装机、可再生能源占比77%等定量目标与时间表
content:
Markets & Policy
Türkiye’s energy vision for 2040 aims to increase renewables’ share of the country’s total installed capacity to 77%, from around 63% today.
Patrick Jowett
06 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Utility-scale
Türkiye is aiming to reach an installed solar and wind capacity of 175 GW by 2040, according to targets set out in its new national energy policy.
The country’s Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar presented Türkiye’s national energy vision for 2040 earlier this week ahead of the start of COP31, to be held in Antalya, beginning November 9.
The plan projects total installed power capacity will rise from the current 123 GW to 281 GW, with renewables share of total installed capacity increasing from the current 63% to 77%.
Speaking during a launch event, Bayraktar said Türkiye will reach its 281 GW target with support from its Renewable Energy Resource Areas (YEKA) program and with the build out of international projects, capacity increases and renovations, and additions of hybrid capacities at existing plants.
He added that distributed systems up to 1 MW in size will be another key focus.
“Wars and crises have shown that distributed production has become very vital,” Bayraktar explained. “That is, on-site production, on-site consumption. Energy infrastructures become the main target in wars. Our distribution of production also has a strategic meaning. We aim to establish small power plants under 1 MW more intensively.”
Bayraktar said reaching the 281 GW target will require around $190 billion, approximately $100 billion of which is expected to go towards rolling out additional solar and wind projects.
Another feature of the plan is increased flexibility and storage, with Bayraktar stating Türkiye needs 140 GWh of storage capacity. He also pointed to increased interconnection, with plans to take interconnection capacity from 5.4 GW today to 15 GW by the end of next decade.
Additional targets set out by the vision include reaching 92% national production and 36% electrification by 2040. It also plans to reach a nuclear capacity of 10 GW.
Türkiye’s new energy roadmap follows an ongoing target to reach 120 GW of combined solar and wind capacity by 2035.
The country’s cumulative solar capacity stood at around 26.9 GW by the end of the first half of 2026, after adding
2.1 GW across the first six months of the year
4.7 GW across 2025
Türkiye’s most recent YEKA tender concluded earlier this week, awarding
785 MW of solar capacity
across 11 projects.

title: U.S. startup secures $9 million to scale production of 22.33%-efficient perovskite solar modules - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
U.S.-based RadianX has secured $9 million in financing to scale production of perovskite solar modules for connected devices and IoT applications. The company plans to establish an automated 6 MW production line.
Lior Kahana
06 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
US-based perovskite solar module manufacturer RadianX has secured $9 million in combined venture capital and project financing. The company plans to use the funding to scale up production of modules for connected devices, including sensors, wearables, and asset trackers, with a new automated production line featuring 6 MW of annual capacity.
“Most connected devices still depend on a battery that someone has to replace,” said Josh Douglas, co-founder and chief operating officer of RadianX. “Our job is to turn that light those devices already receive into power, to drive increased uptime and even reduce or eliminate the battery.”
RadianX’s single-junction perovskite modules are designed to harvest energy from indoor, outdoor, and diffuse light. The company said the modules are available in customized sizes and output voltages, with thicknesses starting at 0.7 mm to enable integration into existing product surfaces. It reported certified efficiencies of 22.33% for a 1.2 × 0.6 m module and 24.24% for a 300 × 300 mm module.
The company’s thin-film technology uses a perovskite absorber less than 1 µm thick, deposited onto glass or film substrates using low-temperature coating processes. RadianX said it can adjust the absorber’s bandgap to optimize energy harvesting under different lighting conditions, including artificial indoor lighting and sunlight. Its modules reportedly achieve a power density of 50 µW/cm² under 500 lux illumination, with a third-party-tested indoor conversion efficiency of 38%.
RadianX offers rigid glass-based modules under its AlphaGlass product line and semitransparent modules under the AlphaVis brand. It is also developing flexible modules under the AlphaFlex name. The company said its technology is intended to provide a continuous power source for low-power electronics, reducing reliance on replaceable batteries in Internet of Things (IoT) applications.
The company also reported third-party durability testing under IEC TS 63163, a technical specification covering photovoltaic modules integrated into consumer products. According to RadianX, its modules have passed testing under all three categories, including Category 3 for applications involving substantial outdoor exposure. The company said accelerated testing supports a projected service life of more than 10 years.
“We’ve shown record certified efficiency on a full-size module and third-party certified durability on the same platform,” Vivian Qu, co-founder and chief executive officer of RadianX, told
pv magazine
. “Our modules are already powering devices indoors and out, and everyone we ship adds to the field data the industry needs.”
The seed funding round was co-led by SOSV and Twynam, with participation from One Small Planet, Sahsen Ventures, Avila VC, California Innovation Fund, quantumEDGE, Riceberg Ventures, and Alumni Ventures.
Manufacturing partner Pacific Union Technology Precision Manufacturing (PUT) will also contribute financing for a dedicated production line targeting connected devices and IoT applications. The planned expansion is intended to support the transition from smaller-scale manufacturing to automated module production.

title: Longi achieves 35.31% efficiency in perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell based on self-assembled molecules - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Longi has developed a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell with a certified efficiency of 35.25% by using specially engineered molecules to improve interface quality and charge extraction. The device also demonstrated enhanced operational stability, retaining 94% of its initial efficiency after 1,500 hours of continuous operation.
Emiliano Bellini
06 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Schematic of the tandem solar cell
Chinese solar module manufacturer
has developed a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell using specially designed molecules that suppress excessive molecular stacking while maintaining efficient charge transport.
“This molecular design promotes the formation of a uniform, well-organized self-assembled monolayer (SAM), even on rough, pyramid-textured surfaces,” Longi researcher Bo He told
pv magazine
. “By balancing molecular packing and surface coverage, the engineered interface improves energy-level alignment for faster charge extraction, reduces defects through molecular flexibility, and provides a stable foundation for the growth of high-quality perovskite films.”
The researchers explained that conventional SAM molecules often suffer from excessive aggregation, resulting in uneven coverage on textured silicon surfaces. To address this limitation, they designed molecules with controlled molecular twisting and conjugation. They developed four SAM derivatives – TC0, TC1, TC2 and TC3 – based on the commonly used 4PACz molecule.
TC2 offered the best balance between molecular packing, substrate adhesion and charge transport, as its structure combines a conjugated backbone with a moderately twisted phenyl side group. Molecular simulations showed surface coverage of 83.1%, compared with 75.0% for TC1 and 73.3% for TC3. Experimental measurements confirmed that TC2 achieved more than 80% coverage and exhibited strong anchoring stability.
The improved molecular arrangement also enhanced the electronic properties of the interface between the indium tin oxide (ITO) layer and the perovskite absorber. In particular, TC2 modified the ITO work function and provided favorable energy-level alignment for efficient hole extraction. This strengthened the internal electric field, accelerating charge separation and transport, while improved interface coverage reduced defects and suppressed charge recombination.
The analysis also showed that TC2 promoted slower, more controlled perovskite crystallization, producing larger, more uniform grains with higher crystallinity. The resulting films exhibited improved phase uniformity and reduced nonradiative recombination. Photoluminescence measurements showed a quantum yield of 1.46% and a quasi-Fermi level splitting of 1.292 eV, the highest values among the tested SAMs.
Using this molecular engineering approach, the researchers fabricated a two-terminal monolithic tandem solar cell combining a perovskite top cell with a heterojunction (HJT) bottom cell.
The device features a textured silicon bottom cell coated with an ITO recombination layer, followed by a TC2-based SAM serving as the hole-selective contact. The perovskite absorber is deposited on the SAM and covered with a lithium fluoride (LiF) interlayer, a fullerene (C60) electron transport layer and a tin oxide (SnOx) buffer layer. The stack is completed with a transparent indium zinc oxide (IZO) electrode, a silver (Ag) contact and a magnesium fluoride (MgFx) optical coating.
Under standard test conditions, TC2-based devices achieved an average open-circuit voltage of 2.007 V and a fill factor of 84.30%, outperforming cells based on 4PACz, TC1 and TC3. The champion device reached a power conversion efficiency of 35.31%, with a short-circuit current density of 20.82 mA/cm2, an open-circuit voltage of 2.007 V and a fill factor of 84.53%.
Independent testing by China’s National Center of Inspection on Solar Photovoltaic Products Quality (CPVT) certified a reverse-scan efficiency of 35.25%, a fill factor of 84.98% and a stabilized efficiency of 35.13%. External quantum efficiency measurements confirmed effective light absorption and current generation in both subcells.
Stability tests also demonstrated improved resistance to light-induced degradation and phase segregation in TC2-based perovskite films. The tandem devices retained 94% of their initial efficiency after 1,500 hours of continuous operation under the ISOS-L-1 protocol and 82% after 1,000 hours at 65 C under the ISOS-L-2 protocol.
“Overall, the results demonstrate that optimized molecular interface engineering can simultaneously improve the efficiency, charge transport and operational stability of perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells,” He said.
The cell technology is described in “
Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
,” published in
. Researchers from China’s
Soochow University
Northwestern Polytechnical University
Hong Kong Polytechnic University
participated in the study.
The new development builds on a series of advances in molecular interface engineering for perovskite photovoltaics. In September, an international research team involving Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Northwestern Polytechnical University
developed a symmetry-breaking molecular strategy
that improved SAM coverage by combining symmetric and asymmetric molecules. The resulting inverted perovskite solar cell achieved an efficiency of 26.32%, with a certified value of 25.67%, while retaining 93% of its initial performance after 1,150 hours of operation.
In December 2025, researchers led by Northwestern Polytechnical University
developed a perovskite-silicon tandem cell
with a certified efficiency of 31.71%. Their approach relied on chemical polishing to selectively remove residual lead iodide from the perovskite absorber, reducing recombination losses and improving film uniformity. Around the same time, a team led by Soochow University
achieved 32.3% efficiency
using a steric-complementary interface design combining small, flexible molecules for defect passivation with larger molecules providing protection against environmental degradation. The device achieved a certified efficiency of 32.12%.
More recently, Longi and Soochow University
developed a 34.0%-efficient tandem cell
using a dual-anchored interface incorporating zirconium oxide (ZrO2) nanoparticles between the transparent conductive oxide and the SAM. The approach reduced interfacial recombination and leakage while maintaining efficient charge extraction. The device achieved an open-circuit voltage of 1.997 V and retained 84% of its initial efficiency after 2,000 hours of operation.
Longi has also continued to advance tandem cell efficiency. In April 2025, the manufacturer
achieved a certified efficiency of 34.85%
for a two-terminal perovskite-silicon device, using a bilayer passivation strategy based on lithium fluoride and ethylenediammonium diiodide. In July 2026, the company
raised its tandem cell efficiency record to 35.5%
, with the result independently certified by the European Solar Test Installation (ESTI).
Alongside its tandem research, Longi has made progress in conventional crystalline silicon technology. In November 2025, the company
disclosed the technical details of its 27.81%-efficient silicon solar cell
, based on a hybrid interdigitated back-contact architecture combining passivated tunneling contacts, dielectric passivation layers and optimized carrier transport.

title: New model shows how shredding methods impact battery material recovery
content: Fraunhofer has developed a modeling tool that lets battery recyclers compare the cost and carbon emissions of different processing methods before changing a production line or scaling up a plant. The tool follows materials through each stage of recycling, showing how a decision such as switching shredding methods can affect the quality of the recovered material and the work required to process it.The model comes from a recent study by the EU’s Safeloop research project, which found that recycling lithium-ion batteries in Europe resulted in an average loss of about €1.90 per kilogram of battery pack under the conditions it examined.Transporting hazardous goods, dismantling packs and uncertainty over how much material could be recovered were among the main factors weighing on the economics.Following materials through the recycling chainFraunhofer’s Modular Lifecycle Tool draws on a database of individual processing steps and technologies. Recycling companies, equipment providers and battery manufacturers can use it to assemble a processing chain based on the composition of the batteries they expect to handle and the amount of material they plan to process.Shredding is one example of where a change can have consequences further down the line. Different methods can alter the quality of the material that reaches the next stage, changing how much work is needed to separate and recover it. By tracking those flows, the model lets users compare the impact of a shredding method across the entire chain.Factoring in location and plant utilizationThe tool links those material flows to estimates for energy use, carbon emissions, capital investment, and operating costs.It also accounts for disposal costs and potential revenue from recovered raw materials, allowing companies to see how a change in recovery rates affects both what they spend and what they can sell.Users can also factor in local labor costs, the regional electricity mix, and how much of a plant’s capacity they expect to use.Changing the amount of material processed or the efficiency of a separation step shows how costs and emissions shift at later stages. That allows companies to see where expenses or emissions are concentrated and how those results change when the plant handles more material.Testing new methods before scaling up“With this tool, we aim to make different recycling concepts comparable on a common basis and thereby create a robust foundation for technological and strategic decisions,” said Benedikt Gruber, a research associate at Fraunhofer FFB.For an existing plant, that could mean comparing its current process with one that uses a different separation technology. A company evaluating a new plant could use the same framework to compare processing routes under different assumptions about throughput, battery composition or local electricity supply.Fraunhofer developed the tool through a consortium study with recycling, plant engineering and consulting partners. The framework is set to expand to cover more battery chemistries, more detailed regional data and different regulatory scenarios. Those additions would let users model a wider range of battery inputs and examine how costs and emissions could vary with plant location and the rules under which it operates.

title: US: Meta agrees to lock 250 MW clean power from Arkansas solar farm
content: Meta, the parent company of popular social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and messaging services like WhatsApp, is championing a 250-megawatt (MW) solar power project in Arkansas. The tech giant has agreed to purchase the cleaner electricity the farm generates.​The solar farm is being developed by EDP Renewables North America (EDPR NA), an American subsidiary of a Portuguese-Spanish Renewable Energy Company.​On Wednesday (November 4), the company broke ground on Cypress Knee Solar in Chicot County, towards the southeastern end of the state. The project is expected to be completed in the next two years, said officials.​Capacity boosts to 545 MWEarlier in May, Meta and EDPR NA announced the deal. Under the agreement, the tech company signed a pact to support the clean energy the latter produces. Cypress Knee is the third such project among them, with Meta’s commitment to buy 545 MW from EDPR NA.​To offset its carbon emissions, Facebook and Instagram’s parent company pledges long-term power purchases of cleaner energy. This contributes to the company’s larger goal of matching 100 percent of its annual electricity use with renewable energy generation.​Beyond providing reliable energy to support America’s power grid, the Kansas project is expected to boost jobs and strengthen the state’s economy.​”As energy demand continues to rise, projects like Cypress Knee Solar help strengthen grid reliability while creating jobs, generating meaningful local revenue, and delivering long-term benefits to the communities that host them,” said EDPR NA CEO Sandhya Ganapathy.​The company estimates that the new solar farm project, once completed, is likely to bring $25 million in revenue over its lifetime.Meta’s previous solar power purchases​Last month, the Silicon Valley company also bought long-term power purchase agreements for a 203 MW solar project in Indiana from the Spanish renewable energy company Zelestra.​The project is being built on reclaimed land from former coal mining operations in southwest Indiana and is expected to go live by 2027.​The moves are in line with the company’s efforts to embrace the shift to cleaner energy.​More and more data centers are being built across the country to provide services such as instant search results and streaming videos to hundreds of followers on social media platforms, and they are massive consumers of electricity. With the recent addition of artificial intelligence (AI) services, tech companies are building even larger data centers to train and run AI models in the future.  ​To counter their energy consumption needs from fossil fuels, the tech giants are investing in sustainable energy generation.​Two years ago, Meta secured 300 MW of clean solar energy for its Texan data center from a Boston-based renewable energy supplier, Longroad Energy.​The project, called 1000 Mile, with support from the technology company for the entire output, will provide solar-powered energy for Yoakum County in Texas. It has an output capacity of 300 MWac or 400 MWdc and lies within the footprint of the Southwest Power Pool (SPP).​All energy generated during the 1000 Mile project will be delivered to SPP’s grid, which will then be supplied to Meta’s data center operations, according to a previous report.

title: US rare earth expansion eyes 4x output to hit 6,000 tons of magnets
content: HyProMag USA is weighing three new rare earth magnet plants that could bring its annual output of magnets, alloy powder, and other saleable material to about 6,000 metric tons by 2034. The expansion would build on the company’s planned first plant in Northlake, Texas, and use a shared finishing hub in central Texas to supply US customers.The company announced the results of an independent pre-feasibility study on October 26. Prepared by PegasusTSI and BBA USA, the study examined how HyProMag could scale up domestic production by using both discarded magnets and primary alloy. The Northlake plant is in detailed engineering, with commissioning of its first phase expected in mid-2028.Finished magnets would account for most of the outputThe study projects that the expanded network, including Northlake, could produce around 4,192 metric tons of finished magnets annually by 2034. It could also produce 1,305 metric tons of magnetic alloy powder and 503 metric tons of other saleable material. Together, the new facilities would add 4,474 metric tons of annual output beyond the volume planned for Northlake.The expansion would proceed in phases, with three regional production plants supported by the central Texas hub. The hub would handle manufacturing, finishing and technology work for the network. Its products would include commercial neodymium-iron-boron (NdFeB) magnets for US customers in sectors such as advanced manufacturing, energy and defense.Discarded magnets and primary alloy would feed the plantsThe expansion builds on Northlake’s use of a recycling method called Hydrogen Processing of Magnet Scrap. The wider network would use material recovered from magnets at the end of their service life alongside primary alloy to make new products. HyProMag said using both sources would give it more flexibility in sourcing material as production grows.“Importantly, the platform is designed with the flexibility to utilize primary alloy feedstock alongside recycled materials, providing greater supply chain resilience and supporting long-term operational competitiveness,” CoTec CEO Julian Treger said.HyProMag could also gain access to primary feedstock from Mkango Magnetic Materials under existing supply rights. That would give the company another potential source of material as it expands from recycling magnet scrap to manufacturing finished magnets.Study values the expansion at up to $2.06 billionThe study estimated an incremental post-tax net present value of $1.85 billion to $2.06 billion and a post-tax internal rate of return of 31% to 36%. The projections cover the three proposed plants and the central Texas hub. Northlake is counted separately in the financial analysis, while its planned production is included in the 2034 output target.“The Study indicates the scalability of the HyProMag business model and provides a framework for disciplined growth in the United States using HyProMag USA’s first plant in Northlake,” Mkango CEO Will Dawes said.The study also points to competitive manufacturing costs and the potential to make lower-carbon finished magnets. The expansion remains at the pre-feasibility stage, with Northlake further along in development as the first facility in the proposed US network.

title: Robots can erase and rewrite their bad memories with MIT's new system
content: MIT builds robot system that lets machines erase and rewrite their own bad memoriesMIT researchers have developed a new memory system that helps robots identify and correct inaccurate descriptions of objects stored in their memory. Called UQ-DAAAM, the system evaluates multiple descriptions of the same object from different viewpoints to determine how confident a robot should be in what it has identified. It then selects additional viewpoints to reduce uncertainty and combines the observations into a more accurate description. The corrected information is stored in the robot’s memory, potentially improving its ability to navigate environments and perform complex tasks.Robots fix memoriesMIT researchers have developed a new artificial intelligence system that allows robots to identify, evaluate, and correct unreliable descriptions of objects stored in their memory. The technology, called UQ-DAAAM (Uncertainty Quantification for Describe Anything, Anywhere, at Any Moment), combines computer vision, language models, and uncertainty quantification to improve how robots recognize and remember objects in their surroundings.The system builds on an earlier robot memory framework called DAAAM, which uses a vision-language model (VLM) to generate detailed descriptions of objects captured by a robot’s onboard cameras. These descriptions are stored in a three-dimensional map-based representation of the environment, allowing the robot to retrieve information about objects when answering questions or performing tasks.However, the original system has limitations when objects are partially visible, distant, or captured in blurry or poorly lit images. Under these conditions, the vision-language model can generate incorrect descriptions. For example, it might mistake a gray chimney for a squirrel on a rooftop. Without a mechanism to correct these errors, the inaccurate information could remain in the robot’s memory and affect subsequent decisions.UQ-DAAAM addresses this problem by introducing a method to measure uncertainty in the descriptions generated by the vision-language model. As a robot moves through an environment, its cameras continuously capture images, often recording the same objects from multiple viewpoints. The new system uses these additional observations to determine whether an existing description is reliable.According to researchers, it first evaluates the model’s confidence in the words it generates when describing a potentially misidentified object. It then measures consistency by comparing that description with captions generated from images of the same object captured from different angles.The system combines these two measurements into a single uncertainty score representing how confident it is in its understanding of an object. If the score exceeds a predefined threshold, UQ-DAAAM identifies the description as potentially unreliable and initiates a refinement process.Improves object recognitionInstead of analyzing every captured image, the system uses a rule-based method to select additional viewpoints that could help reduce uncertainty. For example, if a robot mistakes a chimney for another object, it may select an image showing smoke rising from it to identify the structure more accurately.The researchers mathematically demonstrated that this selection method can identify useful images without repeatedly running the vision-language model. This reduces computational requirements, allowing the system to operate on a moving robot with limited processing resources.Once the additional images have been selected, a large language model (LLM) combines their descriptions into a revised caption. The system gives greater weight to newer descriptions and those containing less ambiguity to produce a more reliable representation of the object. The corrected description is then stored in the robot’s memory for future reference.In testing, the refinement process resolved ambiguities for approximately 92 percent of the objects in the robot’s environment, requiring only two additional captions per object. It also improved object-description accuracy by 5 percent compared with existing state-of-the-art methods.The researchers further found that UQ-DAAAM improved the accuracy of answers to questions about objects, their locations, and when the robot last encountered them.The team now plans to extend the technology to different robotic platforms, including mobile robotic manipulators. They are also exploring whether the system can identify areas of high uncertainty and direct robots to revisit those locations to collect better observations.

title: US Army drops standard mortars from moving drones with new kit
content: The US Army has developed a new kit that lets unmanned aerial systems (UAS) deploy standard mortar rounds. Called the Munitions Air-dropped Lethal Effects Tool (MALET), the Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Armaments Center developed the system. It is designed to convert existing 60mm and 81mm mortar rounds into drone-delivered munitions, reducing the need to procure specialized weapons for unmanned aircraft. The technology could allow soldiers to make greater use of ammunition already available in their inventories.Mortars take flightThe conversion kit allows conventional mortar rounds to be deployed from unmanned aerial systems (UAS), potentially expanding the range of weapons available to drone operators.MALET was developed by the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM) Armaments Center. It is designed to adapt existing 60mm and 81mm mortar rounds for aerial deployment, allowing soldiers to use ammunition already available in military inventories rather than relying entirely on purpose-built drone munitions.According to a statement, Work on MALET began in 2024 after specialists at the Armaments Center’s Fuze and Mortar Divisions identified an opportunity to adapt existing ammunition for unmanned aircraft. The team sought to develop a way to deploy conventional munitions from drones without requiring soldiers to carry out field modifications or manually remove existing safety mechanisms.MALET is designed as a clip-on conversion kit that adds the fuze functionality and aerodynamic stability needed to release a mortar round from an unmanned aircraft. According to the Army, its integration process is non-destructive, meaning attaching the kit does not permanently alter the underlying munition. The conversion can also be reversed by removing the attachment, returning the mortar round to its original configuration. This allows soldiers to retain the option of using an unexpended round as conventional mortar ammunition if it is not dropped or mission requirements change.The approach could offer military units greater flexibility in managing ammunition supplies, particularly when operating drones that require different payload configurations. Rather than maintaining separate inventories of conventional mortar ammunition and specialized aerial munitions, the system is intended to make existing rounds compatible with another delivery method. MALET architecture could also be applied to ammunition beyond the initial 60mm and 81mm mortar configurations.The integrated product team is examining additional concepts, although Gorman described some of the possibilities as “unique” and said they remain largely close-held for now. Mortars were selected for the initial demonstration because the ammunition was relatively mature and aligned with the requirements of larger unmanned aerial systems.Passes live testsThe Armaments Center has conducted test drops at multiple US Army facilities to evaluate MALET’s performance, including its fuze operation and safety features. The team recently completed a successful demonstration involving live 60mm mortar rounds. During the test, a drone released the munition while the aircraft was moving.The mortar rounds oriented correctly after release and detonated within the intended target area, demonstrating the system’s ability to maintain the required flight characteristics and function after an aerial drop.The testing represents an important step in assessing whether existing mortar ammunition can be adapted for unmanned delivery without compromising its original design and safety requirements.The MALET team now plans to distribute the kits during major military exercises in the fall, allowing soldiers to handle and evaluate the system and provide feedback. The development effort has also involved discussions with industry partners, military users, and acquisition organizations.The Armaments Center ultimately intends to validate the technology and transition it to industry partners and the Army‘s acquisition community. This approach is intended to support wider production and rapid fielding while allowing engineers to continue refining the system based on feedback from soldiers participating in tests and exercises.

title: 3D-printed booster delivers 715,000 pounds of thrust at 30% less mass
content: Blue Origin has developed a new rocket engine that delivers more thrust with significantly less hardware. Called Northstar, the liquid oxygen and liquefied natural gas-fueled booster engine produces 715,000 pounds-force of thrust. It also weighs 30% less than the company’s BE-4 engine, despite delivering greater power.The new engine marks Blue Origin’s second booster propulsion system. Its development also demonstrates how advanced manufacturing techniques can simplify rocket engine production. More than 65% of Northstar’s components use additive manufacturing, reducing the number of individual parts and assembly time.Northstar could strengthen Blue Origin’s propulsion portfolio as the company expands its launch capabilities. The announcement also included a major upgrade to its New Glenn rocket, which gains a new third stage for demanding orbital missions.Lighter and more powerful engineNorthstar produces 715,000 pounds-force of thrust, compared with 640,000 pounds-force from the BE-4. That represents a substantial increase in output without adding unnecessary mass. Blue Origin says the new engine cuts overall mass by 30%.The engine also contains 50% fewer parts than its predecessor. Additive manufacturing accounts for more than 65% of its production. This approach allows engineers to consolidate components that traditionally require separate manufacturing and assembly processes.Production speed represents another significant improvement. Blue Origin says technicians can assemble Northstar in less than a day. The company has not disclosed its complete manufacturing process or the engine’s intended launch vehicle.Northstar retains several established elements of Blue Origin’s propulsion architecture. It burns liquefied natural gas and liquid oxygen through an oxygen-rich staged combustion cycle. A single-shaft turbopump handles propellant delivery.That combination connects the new engine with the company’s existing propulsion technology. However, its reduced component count and manufacturing requirements offer a different approach to producing large booster engines.Blue Origin accelerates developmentNorthstar reached development testing just 11 months after receiving program approval. That timeline reflects a development process built around rapid design iterations and in-house manufacturing capabilities.The engine now joins the BE-4 in Blue Origin’s booster propulsion lineup. The company also develops engines for upper-stage and in-space applications, giving it several propulsion options across different mission profiles.The announcement did not specify Northstar’s first flight date or identify a launch vehicle for the engine. Those details will help clarify its eventual role in Blue Origin’s launch operations.New Glenn gains third stageBlue Origin also introduced GS3, a new third stage for its New Glenn rocket. The addition expands the vehicle’s ability to reach demanding orbital destinations without relying on additional spacecraft propulsion.GS3 supports direct insertion into geostationary orbit (GEO) and trans-lunar injection (TLI). Its performance varies with New Glenn’s configuration. The 9×4 vehicle can carry up to 14 metric tons to GEO and 20 metric tons to TLI.The 7×2 configuration supports up to 8 metric tons to GEO and 10 metric tons to TLI. These capabilities could serve commercial satellite operators and government customers. GS3 already has a contracted cislunar mission scheduled for 2028.The stage uses Blue Origin’s BE-7 engine, which delivers more than 460 seconds of vacuum-specific impulse on GS3 mission profiles. It also supports multiple burns and extended coast periods for complex orbital maneuvers.Blue Origin has completed an important structural test for the stage. Engineers pressurized its composite liquid hydrogen tank to 100% of maximum expected operating pressure for 2.5 hours. They subsequently reached 150% of that pressure for 10 minutes.

title: Claude's personal finance tool analyzes accounts and spending patterns
content: Anthropic has introduced a Personal Finance feature in Claude that allows users to connect their bank and credit card accounts and ask questions about their money in everyday language.The feature can analyze account balances, transactions, spending patterns and upcoming payments, helping users understand their finances without manually checking multiple banking apps.Personal Finance is rolling out in beta this week for Claude Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the US. Users can connect accounts through Plaid, a financial technology service that links applications with banks.Anthropic said the feature provides read-only access, meaning Claude cannot move money, manage accounts or make investments on a user’s behalf.The company is positioning the feature as a way to make financial information easier to understand, rather than as a financial management or investment service.Track spending across accountsUsers can ask Claude questions such as “Where did my money go this month?” and receive a breakdown of their spending across connected accounts.In one example shared by Anthropic, Claude analysed $4,309.37 in monthly expenses, identifying rent and utilities as the largest spending category and $1,024.51 spent on food and drink.Users can then ask follow-up questions to compare their spending with previous months, identify recurring payments or check how much money will remain before their next payday.Claude can also flag unusual transactions, duplicate charges, unexpected fees and bills that have gradually increased. Users can ask broader questions, including whether they are spending more than they earn or how much they have paid in credit card interest.The feature can also generate weekly spending charts, payment calendars and custom dashboards based on the financial information users want to track.Anthropic said Claude can explain unfamiliar financial terms, such as annual percentage rates (APR), and calculate the interest charged across connected accounts.Read-only access protects accountsPersonal Finance connects to bank accounts through Plaid. Users sign in directly with their financial institution and approve the requested access, rather than sharing their banking passwords with Claude.For accounts users choose to connect, Claude can access the bank’s name, account name and type, the last four digits of the account number, balances, credit limits, and up to two years of transaction history.Anthropic said conversations within the Personal Finance hub will not be used to train its models. Users can also unlink an account at any time, ending Claude’s access to its data.The company cautioned that Claude can make mistakes in its responses and advised users to check important figures with their banks. It also said the feature is not designed to provide investment advice.Personal Finance is an early step in Anthropic’s broader plans for financial services. The company said it is exploring ways for Claude to work alongside licensed professionals and regulated firms to support more complex financial decisions.Anthropic has invited banks, wealth managers and other financial services companies to help shape these future capabilities.

content: The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) has created a new task force to address criminal threats involving super intelligence (SI), putting federal prosecutors and investigators at the center of America’s emerging technology strategy. The initiative will target foreign adversaries and domestic actors who exploit advanced systems for unlawful purposes.The DOJ Super Intelligence Task Force (DOJ-SITF) will also coordinate with the White House’s Super Intelligence Force (SIF). Its mandate extends beyond enforcement to supporting American technological leadership and protecting domestic innovation.Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss will serve as co-chairs. The department will bring together several law enforcement and legal divisions to oversee the initiative.Federal agencies coordinate enforcementThe task force will coordinate criminal investigations and civil enforcement involving SI across the Justice Department. Its members will also resolve overlaps between investigations handled by different DOJ divisions and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices.Federal prosecutors may need to notify the task force before opening certain investigations. They must also provide notice before pursuing charges or finalizing resolutions in relevant cases, when requested.DOJ LAUNCHES SUPER INTELLIGENCE TASK FORCE ⬇️@POTUS Trump has made clear that “America stands at the forefront of a new technological revolution in intelligence,” and the Department will be a leader in safeguarding against malicious SI actors.“The SI Task Force at the… pic.twitter.com/u0aW2eXcLS— U.S. Department of Justice (@TheJusticeDept) November 5, 2026The DOJ-SITF will establish enforcement priorities focused on public safety and preventing technological misuse. It will also develop prosecution guidance for unlawful SI-related activities.Its responsibilities include evaluating corporate compliance measures. The department wants companies to maintain strong internal controls that prevent advanced systems from being exploited.Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department would work with SI Force Chair Jay Clayton. Their partnership aims to protect critical technologies from domestic and foreign threats.Blanche also warned that authorities would pursue individuals who misuse SI against American taxpayers. That includes threats targeting critical infrastructure and national security.Existing AI task force absorbedThe new initiative will absorb the DOJ’s existing Artificial Intelligence Task Force, announced by Attorney General Pam Bondi in January 2026. That body will no longer operate independently.Its personnel, ongoing work, reporting responsibilities, and existing materials will transfer to the new organization. The consolidation places the department’s existing technology enforcement efforts under one structure.The DOJ-SITF will also serve as the department’s primary contact for the SIF. It can coordinate with other federal departments and agencies when necessary.Innovation remains a priorityThe memorandum establishing the task force also gives it a role in shaping future policy. Through the Offices of Legal Policy and Legislative Affairs, members will advise on legislative and regulatory proposals.The stated objective is to encourage domestic Super Intelligence development without imposing burdensome regulations. The department also wants to strengthen corporate oversight and deter unlawful applications.Woodward described the initiative as part of the DOJ’s broader public safety mission. He said the task force would support technological progress while preventing its misuse.Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss pointed to another responsibility. He said the department must use existing law enforcement powers to deter improper conduct and improve reporting on technological risks.The task force brings criminal enforcement, national security oversight and technology policy under one umbrella. Its effectiveness will depend on how federal agencies identify emerging threats and respond to companies or individuals that cross legal boundaries.

title: Google's Wyoming data center plan pairs gas power with carbon capture
content: Google plans to develop a 702-megawatt (MW) natural gas fuel-cell project with carbon capture and storage (CCS) to support its first data center in Wyoming, as part of a long-term $17 billion investment in the state.The project, announced in partnership with American Electric Power (AEP), Tallgrass Energy, Black Hills Energy and Related Digital, is expected to become the largest planned commercial-scale fuel-cell development of its kind.The fuel cells will be manufactured in the US by Bloom Energy and will convert natural gas into electricity through an electrochemical process. Google said the development will help reduce emissions and water use associated with powering its data infrastructure.Fuel cells pair with CCSThe project will use CCS technology to capture a large majority of its carbon emissions and transport the captured carbon dioxide for permanent geological storage at Tallgrass Energy’s nearby Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub.The hub is being developed to support commercial-scale carbon dioxide storage in the state. Google said the Wyoming project builds on its first US carbon capture and storage agreement, announced last year, and brings its total contracted CCS capacity to nearly 1 gigawatt.The company is also sourcing electricity from natural gas generators operated by Tallgrass Energy and Black Hills Energy. Separately, it is conducting a technical front-end engineering and design study to assess the possibility of fitting Tallgrass’s combined-cycle gas turbines with CCS technology.These arrangements form part of Google’s broader effort to secure power for its expanding data center infrastructure while reducing the carbon emissions associated with natural gas generation.However, the fuel-cell development will still use natural gas, and the carbon capture system is designed to capture a large majority of emissions rather than eliminate them entirely.Wyoming investment extends beyondGoogle said the $17 billion investment is intended to deliver long-term economic benefits to Laramie County and the wider state. The company expects the project to generate hundreds of millions of dollars in local property taxes for the county and School District 1.Its community investment plans will also support K-12 education, workforce development, STEM programs and skilled-trades training.Following a community meeting attended by more than 200 Laramie County residents, Google and its partners are establishing a Community Council to address concerns about the effects of data center expansion on Cheyenne and surrounding communities.Water use is another consideration for the project. Google said the Wyoming facility will use air cooling to reduce pressure on local water resources, rather than relying on water-intensive cooling systems.The announcement comes as technology companies expand data center capacity to support growing computing and digital infrastructure requirements. Securing reliable electricity has become a major challenge for these developments, prompting companies to explore new generation projects and partnerships with energy providers.Google said it will pay for all the electricity its data centers consume and cover infrastructure requirements directly driven by its growth.

title: US military's 16,000-lb helicopter rescued from altitude of 10,000-foot
content: A powerful helicopter of the U.S. Navy has recently been recovered using CH-53K King Stallion helicopter. The U.S. Marine Corps’ CH-53K King Stallion recovered a downed MH-60S Seahawk from the Sierra Nevada mountains. The nearly 16,000-pound aircraft was recovered by a CH-53K from Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron (VMX) 1 using a “long-line” with a U.S. Marine Corps Helicopter Sling Load rigging and delivered to an airfield at Naval Air Weapons Station, China Lake, California. Because the MH-60S was recovered without incident or damage it will be able to fly again without extensive maintenance.Helicopter recovery utilized specialized rigging configurationThe U.S. Marine revealed that the recovery utilized a specialized rigging configuration developed with the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division (NAWCAD) Cargo Lab and Maritime Industrial Base and NAWCAD Structures Lab.“The hardest part of this recovery wasn’t necessarily lifting the H-60. It was figuring out how to do it safely without causing any additional damage,” said Major Lee Henderson, VMX-1 pilot and lead planner.“We integrated established MH-60S crane-lifting procedures and the hoist sling with a 70-foot long-line to ensure proper load distribution and obstacle clearance.”Because the long-line used in the recovery is longer than a standard U.S. Marine Corps equipment sling line used across the military in sling load operations, the recovery operation presented an opportunity to certify the CH-53K in its use.MH-60S couldn’t takeoff due to angle of terrainThe MH-60S, which belongs to Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 31, landed hard at an elevation of 10,000 feet but had no damage. It was unable to take off because of the angle of the terrain. The remote location and elevation added difficulty getting personnel and equipment to the site – meaning it would be extremely difficult to defuel the helicopter to reduce weight, according to a press release.The King Stallion is the only aircraft capable of performing the recovery of the MH-60S due to the power requirement and restrictive terrain. The goal of the recovery operation was to keep the MH-60S in as “whole” a condition as possible to avoid damage to any part of it. Experts from the Cargo and Structures Lab were brought in to develop the rigging procedures; coordinate testing and certification of the long-line; perform long-line testing and data processing for the final report; and be on-site during recovery, as per the release.The H-60 Fleet Support Team at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina, was also consulted to provide guidance on proper configuration of the MH-60S for lifting and also to assist with weight reduction recommendations.Henderson also highlighted that the CH-53K’s available power, precision flight-control system, and ability to calculate instantaneous power available using real-time engine performance and environmental conditions significantly reduced risk during this complex recovery and enabled precise, efficient execution.The mission demonstrated the effectiveness of an integrated Navy and Marine Corps in an austere environment.

title: NVIDIA's VFlash speeds robot decoding 12x and cuts errors by 61%
content: NVIDIA researchers have developed a new visual planning method that accelerates robot trajectory decoding by up to 12 times, while reducing 3D trajectory prediction errors by as much as 61% in specific tests.Called VFlash, the method allows vision-language models (VLMs) to generate complete robot trajectories and other spatial predictions in a single pass, rather than producing coordinates one at a time.In robot manipulation tests, VFlash also cut overall inference latency by about 80% on NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor and DGX Spark platforms, potentially helping robots respond faster to changing environments.The research addresses a limitation in conventional VLMs, which often generate spatial predictions one coordinate at a time. As robots need to predict longer trajectories, track more objects and process increasingly detailed spatial information, this sequential approach can increase processing time.VFlash instead uses the known structure of visual predictions to generate an entire geometric object or trajectory in one forward pass.In tests involving robot manipulation, the researchers reported that VFlash reduced inference latency from 3,552.7 milliseconds to 703.3 milliseconds on NVIDIA’s Jetson Thor platform. This represents an approximately 80% reduction compared with conventional autoregressive decoding.On DGX Spark hardware, latency fell from 3,356.5 milliseconds to 649.9 milliseconds.Model predicts complete trajectoriesVFlash works by identifying the structure of a requested visual prediction before generating its coordinates. For example, a bounding box has a fixed coordinate layout, while a trajectory can contain a variable number of two-dimensional and three-dimensional points.The model uses a lightweight diffusion-based drafter to predict these coordinates jointly in a single forward pass. Unlike conventional speculative decoding, which checks generated tokens against a target model, VFlash can accept structurally valid visual predictions without requiring token-by-token agreement.The researchers evaluated VFlash across several two-dimensional and three-dimensional robot trajectory prediction tasks. The method reduced prediction errors in multiple tests compared with the underlying autoregressive approach.In three-dimensional trajectory tests, it lowered average displacement error by as much as 61%, depending on the dataset and training configuration.The researchers also tested VFlash on 3D point-motion forecasting, where it predicted the future movement of objects across video frames. Preliminary single-rollout measurements showed approximately 25 times faster generation than autoregressive decoding.Faster predictions aid robotsThe researchers also investigated whether faster visual predictions could improve the performance of downstream robot-control systems.They connected VFlash-generated trajectories to a world action model evaluated on MolmoSpaces, a benchmark for robotic manipulation. The model achieved an average success rate of 70.2% across four task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline system.The largest improvements appeared in pick-and-place and object-closing tasks, where success increased by 11.6 and 12.8 percentage points, respectively.Beyond robotics, the researchers tested VFlash for autonomous driving using NAVSIM and Waymo datasets. The model generated driving trajectories with competitive benchmark performance, while reinforcement learning further improved its planning results.The findings suggest that generating detailed visual plans more efficiently could help physical AI systems respond faster to changing environments while maintaining spatial accuracy.The research, titled VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding, was published by NVIDIA researchers and collaborators in November 2026.

title: US Navy to equip warships with 3,000-mph PAC-3 MSE missile hunters
content: The US Navy is working to bring the Army’s PAC-3 MSE interceptor aboard its warships, giving the fleet another option against incoming missiles and other aerial threats. Lockheed Martin received a second-phase development contract in late September to integrate the interceptor with the Navy’s Aegis Combat System.The effort will adapt the Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) for launch from the Mk 41 Vertical Launching System (VLS). Lockheed Martin is targeting land-based flight tests in 2027, followed by shipboard trials in 2028. The Navy aims to field the integrated system by 2029.The award follows an earlier $93 million contract that established PAC-3 MSE as an official Navy program. Lockheed Martin has also invested $120 million of its own funding to prepare the missile for maritime operations.Adapting the interceptor for shipsMoving PAC-3 MSE from land-based launchers to Navy warships requires significant engineering changes. The missile must work with the ship’s existing launch infrastructure and combat management architecture.Lockheed Martin is developing a new communications architecture with S-band and X-band capabilities. The design will support future upgrades as the Navy adapts its defenses to emerging threats.Engineers are also modifying the missile’s launch sequence timing software. Additional work includes new containerized fire-control software and a redesigned canister compatible with both Mk 41 VLS and PAC-3 MSE.The Mk 41 system presents a particular integration challenge. Its canisters must accommodate the interceptor without compromising the missile during launch. Lockheed Martin recently completed a push-through test to verify that PAC-3 MSE could pass through the Mk 41 canister without sustaining damage.Jason Reynolds, Lockheed Martin’s vice president and general manager for Integrated Air and Missile Defense, said the Navy partnership would bring a combat-proven interceptor into its maritime defense architecture.Testing the naval configurationThe program has already cleared an earlier launch milestone. In 2024, Lockheed Martin and US Department of War offices launched PAC-3 MSE vertically from an Mk 70 VLS launcher.The test also integrated the interceptor with a virtual Aegis Weapon System. It marked the first vertical launch of PAC-3 MSE under an Aegis integration configuration.The upcoming trials will take the effort further. A land-based flight test in 2027 will precede shipboard flight testing in 2028. These evaluations will help validate the integration before the Navy begins fielding the capability.PAC-3 MSE uses hit-to-kill technology, destroying incoming threats through direct impact. Its existing mission set includes tactical ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and aircraft. Lockheed Martin also lists hypersonic missiles among the threats the interceptor can counter.Production faces growing demandThe Navy program arrives as the US military expands PAC-3 MSE production. On July 29, the Army awarded Lockheed Martin a $58 billion contract to accelerate manufacturing.The agreement supports a broader production expansion intended to triple manufacturing capacity. Demand comes from the Army, the Navy’s planned adoption, and international customers.Lockheed Martin is also working with the Army on production improvements across its supplier network. These efforts target manufacturing bottlenecks and component deliveries.The naval variant will share production lines with Army versions at Lockheed Martin’s All-Up Round III facility in Camden, Arkansas. That arrangement will support manufacturing as the Navy moves toward its 2029 fielding target.

title: Submarine-hunters with new modifications to boost US' battle power
content: Submarine hunter aircraft in the U.S. are set to get new modifications, which can boost its operational effectiveness. For this, Boeing has secured a new $119.7 million contract modification from the US Navy. Boeing will now manufacture additional upgrade kits for the P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft operated by the United States and Australia. The latest contract is a significant another step in the modernization of the P-8A Poseidon aircraft, which plays a crucial role in anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime surveillance and anti-surface warfare missions. Submarine-hunter is a multi-mission maritime patrol aircraft“The Boeing Co., Seattle, Washington, is awarded a $119,654,234 cost-plus-fixed-fee modification (P00001) to a previously issued order (N0001926F1095) against a basic ordering agreement (N0001926G1002),” read a contract order issued by the Department of War.“This modification exercises options to procure nine retrofit A-kits, seven for Navy P-8A Poseidon aircraft and two for Royal Australian Air Force P-8A aircraft, incorporating Increment Three Block Two engineering change Proposal Six capabilities. The modification also provides for the installation of four retrofit A-kits and associated government-furnished B-kits on Navy P-8A aircraft.”The Boeing P-8 Poseidon is a multi-mission maritime patrol aircraft excels at anti-submarine warfare, anti-surface warfare, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, maritime domain awareness, and search and rescue. In operation worldwide, the P-8 redefines the standards of multi-mission patrol and reconnaissance in every mission it undertakes.Submarine hunter executes anti-submarine warfare through sensor suiteThe aircraft executes anti-submarine warfare (ASW) through an integrated sensor suite to conduct search, detection, classification, localization, tracking and attack of submarines. The P-8 utilizes a state-of-the-art acoustics sensor suite, sonobuoys, electronic support measures (ESM), inverse synthetic aperture radar (ISAR) and the delivery of torpedoes for sub hunting.The aircraft executes anti-surface warfare (ASuW) through elegant communications and data link systems. This integrated sensor suite conducts search, detection, classification, localization, tracking and attack of naval surface targets, utilizing ESM and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) and delivering Harpoon missiles.The P-8A Poseidon is designed to locate, track and monitor hostile submarines operating across vast maritime areas. Its effectiveness depends on the integration of advanced acoustic sensors, radar systems, communications equipment and mission-management technologies.The P-8A Poseidon is based on the Boeing 737 commercial aircraft platform but has been extensively redesigned for military maritime operations. It combines long-range endurance with advanced sensors, mission systems and weapons integration. The platform performs maritime ISR through a proven sensor suite of radar with ISAR, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), periscope, search and navigation. These systems are optimized for combat-ready maritime patrol in detecting, locating and tracking surface and undersea targets. The aircraft performs a wide range of missions, including submarine detection, maritime patrol, intelligence gathering, surveillance, reconnaissance and anti-surface warfare. title: 72,000-ton British carrier launches attack drones for first time
content: The Royal Navy has tested a new ship-launched strike drone aboard its largest aircraft carrier, HMS Queen Elizabeth. The Nyan One-Way Effector (OWE) completed four launches in the North Atlantic, hitting its designated targets in every attempt.HMS Queen Elizabeth displaces approximately 71,650 tons, making it the largest warship ever built for the Royal Navy. Operating Nyan from a carrier of this scale gives the service valuable insight into integrating uncrewed strike aircraft into major maritime operations.Developed by Callen-Lenz, a BAE Systems subsidiary, Nyan is designed to deliver precision strikes using an uncrewed aircraft. Its successful carrier trials mark another step toward operating expendable strike drones alongside crewed aircraft and other naval platforms.The tests took place during Exercise Neptune Reach B, which explores how uncrewed weapons could support future British carrier strike operations. The Royal Navy now has evidence that Nyan can launch from a major aircraft carrier and execute its assigned strike profile.Testing drones aboard carriersOperating an uncrewed strike aircraft from an aircraft carrier presents challenges beyond simply launching it from a runway. The system must function within a complex maritime environment and integrate with the ship’s aviation operations.Nyan completed four separate launches from HMS Queen Elizabeth during the North Atlantic exercise. All four aircraft reached their designated strike points, according to BAE Systems.The drone has a wingspan of 2.9 meters and offers a relatively compact design for maritime operations. Its one-way configuration focuses on delivering a precision strike rather than returning to the launch platform.The carrier demonstrations follow an earlier maritime launch from the Royal Navy’s experimental vessel XV Patrick Blackett. That test took place during Exercise Neptune Reach A earlier this year.HMS Queen Elizabeth also hosted the Heavy Lift Challenge 3 trials, which saw a Tekever AR5 fixed-wing drone operate from an aircraft carrier for the first time. The aircraft has a 23-foot wingspan and can carry payloads weighing up to 176 pounds. Its potential roles include logistics and intelligence, surveillance, target acquisition, and reconnaissance (ISTAR).Together, the trials give British defense planners more information about launching uncrewed strike systems from different naval platforms.Britain’s hybrid navy ambitionsThe Royal Navy is exploring how uncrewed aircraft could increase the number of available strike assets without relying entirely on conventional crewed platforms.Project Vantage coordinates these efforts across the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force. The initiative aims to accelerate testing and inform decisions about future maritime one-way effectors.Lieutenant Commander David Burton, the Royal Navy’s capability sponsor, said Neptune Reach B provided important insight into future carrier strike operations. He added that the trials would help determine how uncrewed strike drones could operate alongside other capabilities within maritime task groups.The findings will also inform Britain’s Maritime Aviation Transformation program. Its broader objective involves developing a hybrid navy with more operational options.Matt Foster, CEO of Callen-Lenz, described the carrier launches as another demonstration of Nyan’s potential. He said affordable, scalable combat mass could increase the effectiveness of existing military capabilities.Expanding uncrewed strike capabilitiesBAE Systems is developing Nyan within a wider portfolio of uncrewed aircraft. Its FalconWorks research and technology hub supports work on emerging aviation systems and autonomous platforms.The company brings more than 25 years of experience in uncrewed and autonomous technology. Its current strategy focuses on systems that can complement existing frontline aircraft and future platforms.Nyan’s carrier trials provide an early indication of how relatively small strike drones could fit into naval aviation. The four successful launches establish a foundation for further testing.The Royal Navy has not announced an operational deployment date for the system. Future evaluations will help determine how these aircraft could support carrier operations and Britain’s wider maritime strike capabilities.

title: US' thousands of tons of submarines, carriers to get modern propulsion
content: Multiple powerful submarines and aircraft carriers in the United States are set to get advanced systems to boost their performance. For this, Curtiss-Wright Corporation has been awarded contracts valued in excess of $225 million by Bechtel Plant Machinery Inc. The aim is to provide advanced propulsion valves, pumps and instrumentation and control systems for the U.S. Navy’s Virginia-class nuclear powered attack submarine, Columbia-class submarine and Ford-class aircraft carrier programs.Curtiss-Wright will supply critical technology to support ongoing ship construction and fleet maintenance activities.Submarines to get mission-critical products that enhance performance“Curtiss-Wright is proud to provide mission-critical products that enhance the performance, reliability, and readiness of the U.S. Navy’s nuclear fleet,” said Lynn M. Bamford, Chair and CEO of Curtiss-Wright Corporation. “The Company maintains a longstanding partnership with the U.S. Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, consistently delivering highly engineered solutions that contribute to our nation’s strong defense capabilities. Furthermore, Curtiss-Wright remains well positioned to benefit from the administration’s continued strong funding for naval shipbuilding supporting the acceleration of production on its most critical platforms.”Curtiss-Wright is performing this work at its facilities in New York and Pennsylvania within the Company’s Defense Electronics and Naval & Power Segments. Engineering, manufacturing, and testing are currently underway, and will continue through 2030, according to a press release.The latest contract awards reinforce Curtiss-Wright’s longstanding position as a key technology supplier to the U.S. Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program, while highlighting the continuing importance of advanced engineering systems in maintaining the operational capabilities of the American naval fleet.Curtiss-Wright will execute the contracts at its facilities in New York and Pennsylvania through its Defense Electronics and Naval & Power business segments. Engineering, manufacturing and testing activities are already underway and are scheduled to continue through 2030. The work will contribute to both the construction of new naval vessels and the maintenance of existing platforms.Equipment supplied under agreements plays key role in performanceThe equipment supplied under the agreements plays an important role in supporting the operational performance, reliability and safety of nuclear-powered submarines and aircraft carriers. By delivering specialised propulsion and control technologies, Curtiss-Wright will help support the complex engineering requirements associated with the U.S. Navy’s next-generation naval platforms.The delivery of advanced propulsion, pumping and control technologies is an essential part of this broader effort. title: Sound sensors on solar panels measure rain with under 2 mm/h error
content: Scientists have developed a system that uses structure-borne sound sensors and machine learning to measure rainfall without moving parts.The technology could complement conventional rain gauges. The system achieved an average error of 1.88 millimeters per hour,Scientists have developed a new artificial intelligence (AI)-powered rainfall monitoring system that can estimate light rainfall with an average error of just 1.88 millimeters (mm) per hour.The new method, developed by researchers at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Media Technology (IDMT) and Pan Acoustics GmbH, analyzes the tiny vibrations produced when raindrops strike solar panels. It offers a low-maintenance alternative for expanding weather monitoring networks.The system uses structure-borne sound sensors and machine learning to measure rainfall without moving parts. The technology could complement conventional rain gauges by creating dense networks of inexpensive measurement points that capture highly localized rainfall.The researchers demonstrated the approach through the recently completed lokalRAIN project, testing the system in both laboratory experiments and outdoor installations. They are now seeking industry partners for additional pilot deployments to evaluate the technology under a wider range of operating conditions.“We have proven the feasibility of our approach for light rain,” said Jakob Bergner, the project’s scientific director at Fraunhofer IDMT. “Now we want to collect further data for the less frequent heavy rain events and optimize the procedure for different operating conditions.”Turning solar panels into rainfall sensorsThe system attaches structure-borne sound sensors to photovoltaic (PV) modules. Every raindrop that hits the panel generates microscopic vibrations, creating unique acoustic signatures that vary with rainfall intensity.Instead of sending raw sensor data to remote servers, an AI model running on an energy-efficient microcontroller processes the information directly at the measurement site. Only the calculated rainfall values are transmitted, significantly reducing power consumption and wireless bandwidth requirements.Pan Acoustics developed the hardware and software for the wireless communication network. During field testing, the system achieved transmission ranges of about 2.5 miles (4 kilometers) in urban environments, and more than 22 miles (35 kilometers) in rural areas with an unobstructed line of sight, the statement reported.Data collected from multiple sensor nodes were then combined within a central data infrastructure to generate localized precipitation maps.Filling gaps in existing weather networksConventional precipitation monitoring depends on weather stations equipped with dedicated rain gauges, which can be costly to install and maintain. As a result, many regions have relatively sparse monitoring networks that struggle to capture localized storms, where rainfall can vary dramatically over short distances.To validate the new approach, researchers first conducted experiments inside a rain simulator, testing different droplet sizes, rainfall intensities, photovoltaic modules, and sensor placements.They later deployed three outdoor measurement systems at Fraunhofer IDMT in Ilmenau, Pan Acoustics in Wolfenbüttel, and the weather garden at the Technical University of Ilmenau. The collected data were compared with reference rainfall measurements to train and validate the machine learning models.For rainfall rates between 2 and 5 millimeters per hour, the system achieved an average error of 1.88 millimeters per hour, meeting the World Meteorological Organization’s (WMO) Class C accuracy requirement for low-intensity precipitation measurements.From weather forecasts to risk managementThe researchers stress that the technology is designed to supplement rather than replace high-precision precipitation gauges.A denser network of rainfall sensors could improve real-time monitoring of localized downpours and provide valuable data for urban digital twins, allowing municipalities and infrastructure operators to respond more quickly to flood risks. The information could also support drainage planning, insurance risk assessments, and weather forecasting models.Fraunhofer IDMT is also exploring agricultural applications through another project that integrates the sensor network into agrivoltaic systems, enabling farmers to make more targeted irrigation decisions using site-specific rainfall data.Before commercial deployment, the researchers plan additional pilot installations to collect more data during heavy rainfall events and further refine the sensor housing, electronics, and quality-assurance processes needed for production-ready systems.
