title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber with 51% higher exploit success rate
content: OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a specialized cybersecurity model that can identify software vulnerabilities and develop working exploits, while showing improved ability to stay within the boundaries of authorized security testing.The new model scored 48.5% on ExploitGym, a benchmark that tests whether models can exploit specified vulnerabilities in remote targets. This represents a 51% relative improvement over GPT-5.6 Cyber, which scored 32.1%.OpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber also outperforms its general-purpose GPT-6 Astra model on most cybersecurity tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the requests.The company has classified GPT-6 Cyber as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for its predecessor. The classification reflects the model’s stronger ability to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits.Firefox flaws emerge despite testingOne of the most notable demonstrations of the model’s capabilities came from a vulnerability research campaign involving Mozilla’s Firefox browser.OpenAI researchers used GPT-6 Cyber to uncover 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities that Mozilla classified as high severity. The model also identified 30 previously reported issues that were more serious than initially assessed.The researchers provided Mozilla with evidence, reproducible tests, and proposed patches to help its engineers address the flaws. Mozilla has since begun releasing fixes for many of the reported vulnerabilities.OpenAI also developed a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing, in which models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT-6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities, compared with 32% for GPT-6 Astra.Unlike conventional vulnerability assessments that examine source code, the web penetration test required GPT-6 Cyber to identify weaknesses by interacting directly with live web applications. This tests whether the model can discover exploitable entry points using only the behavior and responses exposed by a running service.The model has also demonstrated its ability to reproduce and exploit vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel. It reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 of them. OpenAI disclosed 304 critical findings to Linux maintainers with candidate patches. The company has previously detailed this research separately.Model improves testing boundariesBeyond exploit development, OpenAI has focused on ensuring GPT-6 Cyber respects the limits of authorized security assessments.In its ExploitGym Honeypot evaluation, researchers placed models in isolated environments containing vulnerable supporting services. Although exploiting these services could reveal a task’s flag, doing so was outside the authorized scope.GPT-6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without deployment safety prompts. With the prompts enabled, it achieved 100% compliance. GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 94.49% without the prompts.OpenAI said specialized training helps the model follow researchers’ restrictions, remain within authorized testing environments, and report findings accurately.The company is pairing these capabilities with additional safeguards, including cyber-specific monitoring, restrictions on high-risk activity involving critical infrastructure and human oversight for sensitive workflows.GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. OpenAI plans to expand access to other Daybreak Red customers, while also making GPT-5.6 Cyber available to them.

title: ​New recycling process turns plastic waste into high-performance glue
content: A team of researchers at ETH Zurich has developed a one-step chemical process that transforms common plastic waste, including polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), into high-performance adhesives, offering a potential alternative to conventional recycling methods that degrade plastic quality.​The technique allows scientists to “upcycle” polyolefins, the world’s most widely used plastics, by attaching new polymer chains with tailored chemical functions instead of breaking the materials down into lower-value products.​The breakthrough could help address one of the biggest challenges in plastics recycling. Around 450 million metric tons of plastic are produced globally every year, with polyolefins accounting for roughly half of all plastic consumption. Most are used only once before ending up in landfills or incinerators, while mechanically recycled plastics typically suffer significant quality losses.​Unlike conventional recycling, which melts plastics and often produces darker, weaker materials suitable only for products such as paving slabs or plant pots, the new approach retains the polymer backbone while it adds entirely new properties.“Our adhesive is a first-generation product,” said Tae-Lim Choi, professor of polymer chemistry at ETH Zurich. “In the future, plastics with entirely new properties will be possible.”​From shopping bags to structural adhesivesThe research team, led by Choi, demonstrated the technology by converting discarded plastic bags and bottles into industrial-grade adhesives.According to the researchers, the resulting material can bond metals, glass, and wood with sufficient strength for load-bearing and heavy-duty applications used in vehicle and equipment manufacturing.​The process also opens the door to a much broader range of products. By grafting different polymer chains onto polyolefins, scientists can introduce chemical functionalities that are missing in conventional plastics, including water-attracting groups, acids, bases, or highly specific reactive chemical groups.​This versatility could enable applications reaching far beyond adhesives, researchers said.Light-triggered chemistry replaces energy-intensive recycling​One of the biggest hurdles in recycling polyolefins, which include polyethylene and polypropylene, is their chemical simplicity. Because they consist almost entirely of carbon and hydrogen atoms, they lack the reactive sites needed for selective chemical recycling into their original monomers.​As a result, today’s chemical recycling largely relies on pyrolysis, an energy-intensive process that randomly breaks plastics apart at high temperatures to produce petroleum-like feedstocks. These feedstocks must then undergo additional processing before they can be turned back into new plastics.​The ETH Zurich process takes a different approach.​Instead of breaking the polymer apart, the researchers dissolve plastic waste in a chlorinated solvent and expose the solution to short-wavelength light. The light generates highly reactive chlorine radicals that activate carbon atoms along the polymer chains without destroying them.These activated sites then serve as anchors where new polymer chains can grow, letting researchers customize the material’s properties in a single reaction.The method requires neither expensive catalysts nor high processing temperatures, making it considerably simpler than many advanced plastic recycling technologies currently under development.​Researchers also say the reaction can be finely controlled by adjusting both the degree of chlorination in the solvent and the wavelength of the light, granting precise control over how many grafting sites form on the plastic.​Potential uses go beyond adhesivesETH Zurich has patented the technology and nominated it for the university’s Spark Award, which recognizes its most promising patent applications.​Since the patent was published six months ago, the researchers said they have already begun working with industry partners.​One collaboration is exploring food packaging made from modified polyolefins that not only remain waterproof but also provide improved oxygen barriers, helping reduce oxidation and freezer burn compared with conventional polyethylene and polypropylene packaging.​The adhesive developed in the study could also improve recycling itself. According to senior scientist Hongsik Kim, the material could serve as a binder that strengthens low-grade recycled plastics, creating more durable, higher-value products instead of repeatedly downcycling them.

title: ​Chinese team's slurry boosts capacity of manganese batteries by 409%
content: Chinese researchers have developed a new strategy to improve the capacity of manganese-based semi-solid battery systems.​Using the new method, scientists at Shanghai University reported a 409 percent boost in battery capacity over the reported manganese-sulfate (MnSO₄)- based electrolyte benchmark when they switched to a Manganese dioxide (MnO₂) semi-solid slurry electrolyte.​The significant improvement in capacity was observed even when the systems were operated at higher current densities.​These modifications could make them a suitable candidate for large-scale energy storage systems, researchers said.Bottlenecks of traditional Mn-battery systemsConventional manganese-based systems have been a preferred choice for battery materials as manganese is environmentally safe, low-cost, and is abundantly available.​But the traditional redox-based batteries have limited solubility in electrolyte and restrict the amount of energy they can store.​The alternative solid MnO₂ could overcome the challenge as it increases the active-material content. However, these semi-solid flow batteries typically cannot charge or discharge as quickly as desired because the chemical reactions occur slowly. This makes them unsuitable for operations at high charge-discharge rates,​To overcome the two limitations of the conventional Mn-based systems, the team, instead of relying solely on dissolved manganese salts, added solid MnO₂ into the electrolyte. This resulted in a slight change in the electrochemical reaction pathway, the study reported.​”During discharge, solid MnO₂ is electrochemically converted into soluble Mn²⁺, allowing the battery to access more active material without being constrained by the initial solubility limit,” the researcher said.Mn solids enhance capacity​This innovative way of increasing the amount of active manganese helped reduce the common-ion effect that impacts sulfuric acid electrolytes, limiting their solubility.​The approach drastically improved capacity: a slurry mix with 4 Molar (M) MnO₂ achieved a soluble manganese concentration of 3.76 M. According to the study, this increased the battery’s storage capacity to 156.2 ampere-hours per liter (Ah L⁻¹), a 409 percent improvement over the MnSO₄-based electrolyte used as a benchmark.​Performance of these new battery systems at higher current densities was also enhanced. The battery storage capacity was retained above 151 Ah L⁻¹ at the same slurry concentration when a current density of 30 milliamperes per square centimeter (mA cm⁻²) was applied, the study reported. These retained energy efficiencies exceeded 71 percent at the said current density.​The researchers said these operating current conditions are 30 times those previously reported for MnO₂-based semi-solid redox flow batteries, showing that high active-material loading does not necessarily come at the expense of reaction rate.​The researchers also discovered why the battery performs better over time.​During charging, the MnO₂ inside the battery changes into a more reactive form that speeds up the chemical reactions needed to store and release energy. This shift allows the battery to operate efficiently at higher charging and discharging rates while maintaining a high storage capacity.In their lab tests, a battery using a 1 M MnO₂ slurry completed 100 charge-discharge cycles with about 99 percent Coulombic efficiency and 76 percent energy efficiency. However, the researchers said further work is needed to reduce capacity loss caused by manganese crossover and particle buildup.​The findings were published in Nano-Micro letters.

title: 300 MW mobile turbines to reach US amid soaring electricity demand
content: A US energy giant will deliver a total of 10 mobile turbines capable of generating up to 300 megawatts (MW) of electricity to a US customer amid growing demand for reliable power across the country. New York’s New Fortress Energy (NFE) announced the deal on Thursday, October 29. As part of it, will lease the turbines to the undisclosed investment-grade firm for an initial period of five years. According to the company, the equipment will be delivered in stages, starting in the fourth quarter of 2026. The final deliveries are expected in the first quarter of 2027. The deal is set to bring in more revenue from NFE’s existing equipment.Wes Edens, NFE’s CEO, stressed the significance of the agreement. “We evaluated several opportunities for these turbines, and we believe that partnering with an investment-grade counterparty in the United States best aligned with NFE’s priorities,” he added. Mobile energy capacityMobile turbines are a useful alternative to traditional power plants. The reason for this is that they can be transferred to locations where additional power is required and supply extra electricity during periods of high demand.Under the agreement, the 10 turbines have a combined generation capacity of up to 300 MW. Still, NFE has not disclosed their models, fuel requirements, or where they will operate. The firm also did not identify the US customer or specify how the electricity would be used.The Altamira Fast LNG 1 (FLNG 1) located offshore of Altamira, Mexico.Credit: New Fortress Energy / YouTube ScreenshotNFE stressed that the deal follows an evaluation of several potential opportunities for the equipment. It selected the US customer as the agreement aligned with its financial and operational priorities. “It provides the company significant, high-quality cash flows, puts our assets to work more quickly than alternative uses, and serves the growing demand for power in the USA,” Edens explained in a press statement. However, he did not disclose the financial value of the partnership or the expected lease payments. LNG facility restartAt the same time, NFE also shared an update on its FLNG 1 liquefier. The floating facility is located offshore of Altamira, Mexico. It uses gas from the Sur de Texas-Tuxpan pipeline to produce LNG for customers.The FLNG 1 was shut down following a mechanical problem with its gas turbine. The issue disrupted operations and reduced LNG exports from the site. It consists of three converted jack-up rigs.The company said it remains on track to return to service in the fourth quarter of 2026. However, it did not provide an exact restart date or further details about the mechanical issue affecting the unit.The site, which can produce more than 1.4 million tons of LNG per year, kicked off production in July 2024. Its first shipment followed in August, when the Energos Princess LNG carrier transported the fuel to NFE’s La Paz terminal.NFE later secured USD 700 million in financing for its LNG operations in Mexico. As per online reports, part of the funding will also cover construction of FLNG 2, which will use the same modular technology as FLNG 1.“Our FLNG complex is advancing at a rapid pace as we have now produced LNG at our first unit, and fully financed our second,” Edens concluded. “These are large infrastructure projects that add considerable financial and operational value to our Company and we are thrilled with the progress to date.”

title: Earthquake Faults Can Suddenly Become Almost As Fluid as Water, Study Finds
content:
Earthquakes occur when built-up stress in Earth’s crust is suddenly released, causing the ground to shake. Driven largely by the movement of tectonic plates, these powerful geological events can reshape landscapes, trigger tsunamis, and reveal the dynamic forces constantly changing our planet. Credit: SciTechDaily.com
Scientists have uncovered evidence of an unexpected process that may allow earthquake faults to slip enormous distances.
Rocks along Japan’s Boso Peninsula have preserved evidence of an extraordinary process that may occur during powerful earthquakes. Researchers discovered ancient fault structures suggesting that clay trapped between moving rock surfaces became nearly as fluid as water, potentially allowing the fault to slip enormous distances with little resistance.
The findings, from a research team led by Professor Tetsuro Hirono of Osaka Metropolitan University, could help explain how some earthquakes produce the massive seafloor movements capable of triggering devastating tsunamis.
Ancient Rocks Reveal Evidence of Fluid-Like Movement
The researchers examined exposed rocks that formed in an ancient seafloor environment approximately 15 million years ago. Within an old earthquake fault, they identified unusual wavy and curved layers, along with swirling structures resembling vortices formed by moving fluids.
The team described these formations as “turbulent-flow-like.” Using fluid dynamics to analyze their shapes, the scientists found evidence that a process called thermal pressurization had caused clay within the fault to become fluidized.
Traces of turbulent flow generated during an earthquake are visible as swirls within the rock. Credit: Osaka Metropolitan University
Thermal pressurization occurs when rapid movement along a fault generates intense frictional heat. As water trapped in microscopic spaces within the rock heats up, pressure increases, reducing the frictional resistance that normally keeps the fault surfaces locked together. This weakening can allow much greater movement during an earthquake.
How a Weakening Fault Could Trigger a Tsunami
“Our analysis suggests that the viscosity approached that of water,” Professor Hirono explained. “This would have been a dramatic reduction. The fluidized state would have acted as a form of dynamic lubrication, causing the fault to weaken dramatically. The resulting large-scale slip would have produced a large displacement on the fault near the seafloor, potentially causing a tsunami.”
The mechanism could help explain the extreme seafloor displacement associated with some major earthquakes. In 2011, a magnitude 9.1 earthquake struck eastern Japan, with shaking and fault rupture lasting nearly six minutes. The earthquake shifted the ocean floor enough to generate a devastating tsunami. Although the ancient rocks do not establish whether the same weakening process occurred in 2011, they provide physical evidence of how faults may undergo dramatic changes during seismic events.
Ancient Faults Could Improve Tsunami Risk Assessments
The researchers hope to apply their analytical methods to modern faults, using changes in the viscosity of fault materials to better estimate how far those faults might slip during an earthquake. More accurate assessments of fault movement could improve estimates of potential seafloor displacement and associated tsunami hazards.
“Understanding the change in viscosity in fault-slips may allow us to more accurately recognize the magnitude of fault slips, which would support tsunami mitigation efforts,” Professor Hirono concluded.
Reference: “Coseismic turbulence-like flow of fault material along the shallow portion of a plate-subduction-related fault” by Tatsuru Fukuta and Tetsuro Hirono, 27 June 2026,
Scientific Reports
DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-57630-y

title: Scientists Reveal How a Mysterious Brain Structure Keeps Memories From Fading
content:
A little-known structure deep within the brain may play a crucial role in keeping fleeting information available for thought and decision-making. Credit: Shutterstock
Memories that last only seconds shape everyday thinking, and research in mice is revealing how a small brain structure supports an ability impaired in ADHD and schizophrenia.
To understand a sentence, the brain has to keep earlier words in mind as new ones arrive. Working memory makes that possible, holding information for a few seconds so we can compare it with new information, manipulate it, and use it to guide our behavior.
We rely on it to follow conversations, solve problems, and decide what to do next. Yet sensory information fades within moments once a stimulus ends, leaving the brain with the demanding task of maintaining a usable representation of something that is no longer there.
In mice, researchers at
have found that this ability relies partly on the claustrum, a thin structure deep within the brain between the insular cortex and the striatum. Their findings appear in
Nature Communications
The claustrum supports working memory
The scientists tested mice on tasks that required them to remember either a smell or a touch. Each animal received an initial stimulus, waited several seconds, and then received a second stimulus. The mouse had to determine whether the two were identical or different. By the time the second stimulus arrived, the first was gone, so success depended on retaining information about it during the wait.
Temporarily reducing the activity of claustrum neurons cut the mice’s working memory performance in half. To control these neurons at precise moments during the task, the researchers used techniques including optogenetics. This method uses specific proteins to make selected neurons sensitive to light, allowing scientists to alter their activity through an optical fiber. The intervention helped establish that the claustrum contributes to working memory rather than simply becoming active while another brain region does the necessary work.
“The result was similar regardless of the type of stimulus, olfactory or tactile, and regardless of when the disruption occurred during the waiting period between the two stimuli,” says study co-leader Alan Carleton, Full Professor in the Department of Basic Neurosciences at UNIGE’s Faculty of Medicine. “Moreover, disrupting the claustrum specifically impairs the ability to use temporarily held information to guide behavior, without affecting perception itself.”
Memory persists as neural activity changes
Working memory depends on interactions across a broad network that includes the prefrontal cortex, sensory regions, the parietal cortex, the thalamus, and other structures beneath the cortex. These networks must preserve information while allowing the brain to continue perceiving, thinking, and acting, but how they maintain a representation over time remains largely unknown. The claustrum’s anatomy offers a reason to examine its contribution.
“Its neurons are connected to almost all regions of the cortex, which puts it in a good position to receive and influence information from very different networks,” explains Carleton.
Recordings from the mice allowed the researchers to examine how information was represented in claustrum activity during the gap between stimuli.
“Our live recordings of claustrum neuron activity showed that a trace of the initial information persisted throughout the entire waiting period,” says fellow study leader Ivan Rodriguez, Full Professor in the Department of Genetics and Evolution at UNIGE’s Faculty of Science. “Far from being a static memory, neuronal activity changed over time. Nevertheless, the identity of the stimulus remained sufficiently present to be decoded up to 30 seconds later.”
“Our discovery could help us better understand cognitive disorders in which working memory is impaired, such as schizophrenia or ADHD,” explains Carleton. “Identifying the brain circuits that allow information to be maintained over time is an important step towards understanding how these functions can be disrupted. We now need to determine how the claustrum communicates with cortical networks, and how this interaction preserves the fidelity of the representations held in working memory.”
Reference: “The claustrum contributes to working memory maintenance in mice” by Anindya S. Bhattacharjee, Maxime Juventin, Chieko Huber, Burak Unsal, Jean-Rodolphe Renfer, Ivan Rodriguez and Alan Carleton, 14 October 2026,
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78363-6

title: The Hidden Brain Mechanism That Makes You Love Coffee, Chocolate, Fat, and Sugar
content:
New research reveals how a slow dopamine signal between the gut and brain helps shape our food preferences, teaching us to enjoy certain flavors over time. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists have uncovered a previously understudied dopamine pathway that may explain how we learn to enjoy flavors we initially dislike.
A food can become more appealing even when its flavor stays exactly the same. Researchers at
UC San Francisco
have identified a previously understudied dopamine pathway that helps the brain learn which flavors are worth seeking out based on what happens after nutrients reach the gut.
The study, published November 4 in
, reveals how a slow chemical signal connects digestion with learned food preferences. The mechanism could help explain why people develop a taste for initially unpleasant flavors, including the bitterness of coffee.
How the Gut Teaches the Brain What to Like
Dopamine helps the brain learn which experiences are rewarding, but most research has examined rapid signals that appear within seconds of external cues, such as seeing a favorite meal. The newly studied “slow” dopamine system responds to events inside the body. When digestive sensors detect nutrients such as sugar and fat, they initiate signals that can sustain dopamine release in the brain for several minutes.
“We’ve shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens,” said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.
Coffee provides a familiar example of how this learning may work. Although its bitterness can be unpleasant initially, repeated experiences can teach the brain to associate the flavor with caffeine’s stimulating effects. Once that association develops, Knight explained, “that coffee starts to taste a lot better.”
A Hidden Dopamine Signal in the Amygdala
To isolate the brain’s response to nutrients from its response to taste, Knight and James Grove, PhD, who was then a graduate student, delivered sugar water or a milkshake-like liquid directly into the stomachs of mice. They simultaneously measured dopamine release throughout the brain.
Nutrients entering the stomach produced a strong, sustained dopamine response in the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA. Although researchers already knew this region received dopamine signals, their role in learning about food was unclear.
“We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role,” Knight said.
Experiments Reveal How Food Preferences Form
The researchers next tested whether the pathway was necessary for learning. When they blocked it, the mice continued eating normally but could no longer learn that a particular unfamiliar flavor was associated with calories. This showed that the pathway was important for forming food preferences rather than simply controlling food consumption.
In a separate experiment, the researchers artificially stimulated dopamine fibers in the BLA after mice sampled a calorie-free flavor. The animals subsequently developed a preference for that flavor, even though it provided no nutritional reward.
Together, the experiments demonstrated that dopamine signaling in this region can teach mice to associate a flavor with the beneficial effects of nutrients. Artificial stimulation could substitute for the signal normally generated when nutrients reach the gut.
An Unexpected Difference Between the Brain’s Two Sides
Human brain imaging provided additional evidence of a similar response. Yale psychologist Dana Small, PhD, reanalyzed an earlier PET study involving 13 men who consumed either a milkshake or a noncaloric drink. Nutrient consumption was associated with dopamine release concentrated in the left BLA.
In another experiment, Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and colleagues used fMRI scans to study 38 adults after glucose consumption. They detected increased activity in the same brain region, although fMRI measures brain activity rather than dopamine release directly.
Both the mouse experiments and human imaging studies showed substantially stronger responses on the left side of the BLA than on the right. This asymmetry was unexpected because brain circuits involved in basic functions such as feeding are generally considered to operate relatively symmetrically. Knight’s laboratory is now investigating why the nutrient-related response favors the left hemisphere.
Could Scientists Eventually Change Food Cravings?
Identifying this pathway may provide new opportunities to investigate how food preferences develop and whether they can be modified. One possibility involves GLP-1 medications, which mimic a hormone produced in the gut and can substantially alter eating behavior.
The researchers did not test these drugs, so their effects on the newly identified dopamine pathway remain unknown. Knight has proposed that GLP-1 medications might reduce dopamine signaling triggered by nutrients, potentially making certain foods less rewarding over time.
Such a mechanism, if confirmed, would suggest that future treatments could influence not only hunger and fullness but also the learned associations that make particular foods desirable.
“By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods,” Knight said.
Reference: “The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning” by James C. R. Grove, Anna M. Hakimi, Queenie Li, Jingkun Zhang, Heiko Backes, Bojana Kuzmanovic, Jaewon Choi, Violeta Ubadiah, Longhui Qiu, Zhengya Liu, Dana M. Small, Marc Tittgemeyer and Zachary A. Knight, 4 November 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11229-5
This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

title: A New Era of Bionic Vision? AI Helps Scientists Unlock the Brain’s Visual Cortex
content:
Technology
UCSB’s Michael Beyeler is using AI to improve visual cortical prostheses, or “bionic eyes.” Credit: Matt Perko, UC Santa Barbara
Researchers have used artificial intelligence to improve how a brain implant stimulates the visual cortex of a blind person, potentially advancing the development of bionic eyes.
Artificial intelligence could make future bionic eyes more precise and responsive by improving how electrical signals communicate with the brain. In a study published in
, researchers used deep learning to control brain stimulation in a blind man, producing more accurate neural responses with less electrical current.
The findings could advance visual prostheses that bypass damaged eyes and optic nerves, stimulating the visual cortex directly to generate perceptions of light.
Testing AI in a Blind Participant
Researchers from
UC Santa Barbara
ETH Zurich
, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU) tested the approach in a 27-year-old man who lost his sight following a traumatic brain injury. At a hospital in Spain, a temporary implant containing 96 electrodes stimulated his visual cortex, producing phosphenes, perceived as flashes or shapes of light.
Led in part by UCSB professor Michael Beyeler, the team trained a deep neural network to predict brain responses to different stimulation patterns. The AI model also incorporated measurements of resting brain activity, allowing it to account for changes in the brain’s condition before each test.
Why Brain Activity Matters More Than Electrical Signals
The AI-designed stimulation patterns produced targeted neural responses more accurately and required less electrical current than comparison approaches. Researchers also found that recorded brain activity predicted the participant’s visual perceptions better than the electrical settings alone.
“Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image,” Beyeler said. “But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.”
The implant could both stimulate neurons and record their responses, enabling the AI to learn from actual brain activity. The participant also described perceived flashes, including their brightness, size, shape, and color.
Toward More Personalized Bionic Vision
The technology could eventually help people who lose their sight through injuries or neurological and inherited conditions. Beyeler emphasized those “who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision,” adding, “For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.”
Describing the international research effort as “a true collaboration,” Beyeler said the study demonstrated how computational models could influence experiments involving human participants.
“Building a model in the abstract is one thing,” he said. “Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.”
Although the research remains an early proof of concept, it suggests that future visual prostheses may work better by continuously adjusting stimulation to an individual’s neural responses.
“A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe,” Beyeler said. “It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.”
Reference: “Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex” by Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler and Eduardo Fernández, 7 August 2026,
DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

title: Scientists Spent 7 Years Studying Moth Wings and Discovered Something Unexpected
content:
In a scientific first, Lepidoptera expert Andrei Sourakov has altered the shape of moth wings in a study that suggests moths and butterflies may have independently used the same type of gene to evolve tails. Credit: Andrei Sourakov
A search to change the patterns on moth wings uncovered something unexpected: wider tails, suggesting that evolution may reshape insects’ defenses by modifying features they already possess.
A luna moth’s leaf-like wings help it escape the notice of predators that hunt by sight. Other giant silk moths display prominent eyespots that can make them look threatening. A new study suggests that moving between those appearances can require only a small change in the signals that guide wing development.
Over seven years, Andrei Sourakov hand-reared more than 700 luna (
Actias luna
) and polyphemus (
Antheraea polyphemus
) moths from egg to adulthood. Sourakov is the collection coordinator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History and an affiliate associate professor of entomology at the University of Florida. His findings, recently published in
Evolution & Development
, reveal how treatments during development can alter both the patterns and shapes of moth wings.
Polyphemus moths have hindwing eyespots which are exposed only when the moth is threatened, but their forewings look like leaves, with translucent eyespots resembling holes to make it more convincing. Credit: Andrei Sourakov
The first surprise was wing shape
Sourakov treated developing moths with small amounts of heparin and dextran sulfate. Both are sulfated polysaccharides, molecules made of linked sugars with attached sulfate groups. They increase the activity of a group of proteins called Wnt, which help direct development.
He administered tiny quantities of heparin shortly before and after pupation, when caterpillars enter the pupal stage and undergo their final transformation into adults. Wing patterns are determined during this period. For two years, the treatments failed to produce the changes he was seeking, so he continued adjusting the concentration and timing of the doses.
Luna moth eyespots consist of a translucent membrane surrounding a crossvein and several concentric circles formed by scales of different colors. Credit: Andrei Sourakov
“I kept trying, and eventually, I achieved a single transformation. But it wasn’t of the wing pattern. It was the wing shape. This single specimen was so different that I couldn’t ignore it,” he said.
That specimen was a luna moth whose hindwing tails had grown wider than those of any moth he had previously reared. Scientists think luna moths evolved their long tails to
deflect bat attacks
away from the main part of their bodies.
“I thought, this is very bizarre. Maybe the genes that are normally responsible for wing patterns are here responsible for wing shape, because that’s seemingly the only thing that was transformed.”
Subtle eyespots become striking displays
Further adjustments to the timing of heparin treatment eventually produced changes in both wing shape and eyespots, overturning that initial explanation.
In polyphemus moths, the yellow borders around the two lemon-shaped eyespots on the forewings thickened. Brown scales surrounding those markings, which normally matched the rest of the wings, became whiter. On the hindwings, the black borders around the eyespots expanded. Together, these changes made the markings more conspicuous.
Luna moths underwent a similarly striking transformation. Their round hindwing eyespots took on a squinting appearance and developed thick, dark borders resembling mascara, turning subtle markings into a more noticeable display. Both heparin and dextran sulfate also changed the shape of luna moth wings, something not previously achieved experimentally in Lepidoptera, the group that includes all moths and butterflies.
The study demonstrates how easy it would be for cryptic eyespots to become visually threatening via a slight upregulation of wnt genes by expanding normally constricted pattern elements. WT = wild type, control treatment; Hep 1 = heparin, experimental treatment. Credit: Andrei Sourakov
“Some giant silk moths have eyespots that make them appear threatening to would-be predators. Others look like leaves, with translucent eyespots resembling holes to make it more convincing. What’s amazing to me, and what I learned from this study, is how easy it is for these features to go from one state to another. They do this without big inventions by simply expanding or contracting existing elements to the point where eyespots look completely different. All they need is a slight increase in the amount of certain compounds at the right moment,” Sourakov said.
Moths and butterflies respond differently
Moth and butterfly eyespots occupy different parts of the wings, a clue that they evolved independently. Sourakov’s original goal was to investigate whether the two groups used the same genes to create these markings or had independently arrived at similar designs.
He tested the responses of several giant silk moth species to sulfated polysaccharides, reasoning that similar responses in different species could indicate homologous eyespots, meaning markings with a shared evolutionary origin. Further experiments would be needed to confirm that relationship.
Luna moths stay hidden during the day from visually oriented predators by resembling a leaf. Their eyespots are translucent, resembling holes in the leaves. Credit: Andrei Sourakov
In nymphalids, the largest family of butterflies, eyespots sit along the wing margins. Giving these butterflies heparin early in development can eliminate their eyespots entirely. Yet in Sourakov’s earlier experiments with two giant silk moth species,
their eyespots grew larger
. He interpreted those opposite responses as a clear indication that the moth and butterfly markings evolved separately. After his initial giant silk moth studies were
, he expanded the work to include luna moths, better known for their long tails than their faint eyespots.
Wingless may help build moth tails
The changes in wing shape remain harder to explain, particularly because they have not been observed in butterflies treated this way. One possibility involves how moth and butterfly wings acquire their outlines.
Unlike the wings of other flying insects, which stop growing when they reach a certain size, Lepidoptera wings undergo a process sometimes described as cookie-cutter growth. Cells along the future wing margins die in a controlled sequence, shaping the edges. A protein called Cut helps mediate the signal for those cells to self-destruct, but it does not respond to heparin or dextran sulfate.
The patterns of luna moth wings can be experimentally changed from camouflaged to a much more conspicuous appearance by expanding normally constricted eyespot elements, demonstrating potential for rapid evolution from one state to another. Credit: Andrei Sourakov
Earlier in development, before those marginal cells die, another signaling protein called Wingless helps control the size of individual wing sections between veins. Wingless does respond to the two compounds. However, the
wingless
gene is mostly inactive by the time eyespots begin forming, which is when Sourakov starts his treatments. That timing helps explain why experiments focused on eyespots seldom change the size of those wing sections.
The gene can also be activated when damaged wing cells need repair, allowing new cells to grow in wounded areas. In pipevine swallowtail butterflies, it has another role in the development of their tiny wing tails. A landmark study published in 2010 showed that both
wingless
are active during tail formation in these butterflies.
Heparin slightly changed the shape of luna moth wings, making the tails wider. The study suggests that the gene wingless, normally involved in early wing cell division or cell repair, is also co-opted to create wing tails. WT = wild type, control treatment; Hep = heparin, experimental treatment. Credit: Andrei Sourakov
Sourakov suspects that the same genes may help form luna moth tails. If so, natural selection would have independently recruited
wingless
for the evolution of wing tails in moths and butterflies. Those tails serve different purposes. The small tails of pipevine swallowtails help visually distract birds by contributing to a
false head effect
, drawing attention away from the insect’s actual head. Luna moth tails are much longer, and their shape also affects how the moths fly.
“This is just my deduction, but I think it is very plausible and would explain why in butterflies or other moths we don’t see much change to the wing shape in response to heparin–
wingless
is not turning on at that stage of wing development in most species,” Sourakov said.
The ease of altering wing markings also suggests a possible route for rapid adaptation to a changing environment. If a luna moth’s leaflike disguise stopped protecting it, mutations that made its eyespots more visible could be favored under pressure from hunting birds. In principle, that could shift its appearance within just a few generations.
“If you are a smaller bird or a squirrel, you will think twice before attacking something in the darkness of the forest that looks like the eyes of an owl. Butterflies and moths are masters of such deceptions,” Sourakov said.

title: Scientists Discover Crows Make Decisions Twice As Fast as Humans
content:
Carrion crow (Corvus corone). Credit: Tobias Machts
Quick decisions are essential for birds navigating the world at high speed, and new research suggests crows may have a remarkable advantage over humans in processing what they see.
A crow can make a visual decision in less than a quarter of a second, about twice as fast as a human or monkey. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered this remarkable speed by asking two carrion crows to identify the direction of moving dots on a screen. The birds made their choices in an average of just 235 milliseconds while maintaining a high degree of accuracy.
During the experiment, the crows watched patterns of moving dots on a touchscreen and had to determine whether most were traveling to the left or right. They indicated their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen. Some patterns made the direction easy to identify, while others were much harder to interpret.
“Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows’ decisions were still better than random choices,” Philipp Schmidbauer reports, “and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.”
Crows’ brains distinguish motion in 70 milliseconds
Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder, both from the University of Tübingen’s Institute of Neurobiology, investigated how the birds’ brains could process visual information so quickly. Their study, published in the journal
, examined the activity of individual nerve cells, or neurons, in a brain region called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This area helps birds process information and make decisions, performing a role comparable to that of the prefrontal cortex in humans.
The experiment: The crow needs to decide whether a certain number of white dots on the black screen are moving to the left or to the right at the same time. It indicates its decision by pecking at the corresponding target circle on the monitor, either on the left or on the right, to receive a reward. Credit: Andreas Nieder
The recordings revealed that the crows’ brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared. As the birds processed what they were seeing, neural activity gradually increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. These signals reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the crow ultimately chose.
“These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates,” says Andreas Nieder.
Unlike humans and other primates, birds do not have a layered cerebral cortex. Despite this structural difference, the findings suggest that their brains use similar fundamental principles to make decisions. The remarkable difference is how quickly the crows appear to carry out this process.
Flight and foraging may favor speed
Nieder suggests that this speed may be connected to the demands of birds’ everyday lives, which often require rapid visual processing and precise movements. “Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging,” he says.
Although these demands could help explain the crows’ speed, researchers still need to determine exactly which mechanisms allow birds to make visual decisions so much faster than primates.
Reference: “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain” by Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder, 22 October 2026,

title: A Tiny, Jelly-Like Implant Could Change How We Treat High Blood Pressure
content:
Researchers have developed a soft, 3D-printed implant that uses electrical stimulation to regulate blood pressure without the need for stitches. Credit: Stock
A soft implant that attaches without stitches lowered blood pressure in rats, pointing toward a way to treat hypertension with less damage to surrounding tissue.
Nearly half of all adults in the United States have high blood pressure, a leading cause of heart disease. Medications and changes to diet or lifestyle can help, but roughly one in 10 people with the condition has drug-resistant hypertension. For these patients, controlling blood pressure can become a persistent challenge.
“For many patients, even taking a combination of three to five medicines doesn’t alleviate their high blood pressure,” said Tao Zhou, the study’s corresponding author and the Wormley Family Early Career Assistant Professor of Engineering Science and Mechanics at
Penn State
. “In these cases, bioelectronic devices that use electrical signals to modulate the body’s natural response systems offer a promising form of alternative treatment.” Zhou is also affiliated with Penn State’s Center for Neural Engineering, Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences, and Materials Research Institute.
Even though the team’s new bioelectronic is only about the size of a fingertip, it could offer an effective and biocompatible approach to addressing high blood pressure. Credit: Tao Zhou
Zhou and his colleagues have developed CaroFlex, a soft, stretchy, 3D-printed device that attaches to an artery and delivers gentle electrical stimulation. In a rodent model, it lowered blood pressure while causing much less damage to surrounding tissue, the researchers reported in a paper recently published in
Electrical pulses lower blood pressure in rats
The device works through a pressure-control system the body already has. Specialized nerve endings called baroreceptors detect changes in how much artery walls stretch. They trigger the baroreceptor reflex, or baroreflex, which helps regulate blood pressure, including by changing how tightly blood vessels constrict. Baroreceptors occur throughout the body, with many concentrated in the carotid sinus, a small region near where the carotid artery branches.
This artery carries oxygen-rich blood to the head and neck. Applying electrical stimulation at the carotid sinus can activate those receptors and engage the reflex to lower blood pressure, Zhou explained.
3D printing allows the team to produce bioelectronics faster and with better biocompatibility to the body’s soft tissues than traditional fabrication methods. Credit: Tao Zhou
To test whether CaroFlex could do this in a living animal, the researchers implanted it at the carotid sinus in rats. Sensors on the animals’ bodies monitored blood pressure during a 10-minute testing window. Four of the five electrical frequencies tested reduced blood pressure, with readings falling by more than 15% on average.
When the researchers examined tissues in contact with CaroFlex after two weeks, they found no apparent damage or immune response.
Soft electrodes hold on without stitches
A few commercially available devices already use electrical stimulation to engage this reflex. The engineering challenge is keeping an electrode connected to an artery that continually stretches and shrinks. Conventional devices are generally made from rigid metals and plastics, which do not fit the mechanical behavior of soft tissue well. “These devices are usually held in place with stitches,” Zhou said. “These stitches can cause damage to the devices, and more importantly, the tissues they’re integrated with over time, as arteries stretch and shrink to help move blood around the body.”
CaroFlex is made primarily from hydrogel, a soft, jelly-like material that better matches the tissue’s flexibility. Conductive hydrogels form the electrodes that deliver electrical stimulation, while adhesive hydrogels provide a strong, nontoxic attachment designed to let the device stick painlessly to biological tissue without stitches. The team used 3D printing to build this combination of electrical and adhesive components.
The figure demonstrates the impact CaroFlex had on systolic arterial pressure (SAP), diastolic arterial pressure (DAP) and mean arterial pressure (MAP) in rodent models. The team compared readings taken from before and after stimulation, using four different electrical frequencies, reporting that CaroFlex reduced average levels across all domains. Credit: Tao Zhou
Laboratory tests on tissue samples examined whether the materials could provide both flexibility and a dependable attachment. CaroFlex stretched to more than twice its original size before breaking. Its adhesive film maintained strong, continuous adhesion, including when made from mixtures that had been stored for six months. The researchers also compared CaroFlex with traditional platinum bioelectrodes. By passing electrical currents through each type, they measured how the different materials affected conductivity. CaroFlex adhered more closely to the tissue and provided a more reliable electrical connection than the conventional electrodes, the team reported.
Human trials remain a future goal
With CaroFlex shown to function in living tissue and evidence of tissue compatibility, Zhou said the next steps are to fine-tune its effectiveness and scale up the approach. The eventual goal is clinical trials to test it as a treatment for hypertension in humans.
“Our lab is actively leading several developments in 3D-printed bioelectronics for use across the body, which is exciting,” Zhou said. “This fabrication approach allows us to design, fabricate, and adapt bioelectronics for potential clinical trials and commercial distribution much more efficiently than traditional methods of manufacturing.”
Reference: “3D printable suture-free bioadhesive electronic interface for hypertension therapy” by Marzia Momin, Salahuddin Ahmed, Arafat Hossain, Jia Sun, Xinyi Wang, Basma AlMahmood, Jiashu Ren, Li-Pang Huang, Umar Farooq, John Bisognano and Tao Zhou, 5 May 2026,
DOI: 10.1016/j.device.2026.101150

title: Less Sugar in Early Life Could Protect Your Mental Health Decades Later
content:
A natural experiment involving sugar restrictions suggests that our earliest nutritional environments may influence mental health far into adulthood. Credit: Shutterstock
An observational study links sugar rationing in early life to lower adult anxiety and depression risks, raising the possibility that our earliest diets have lasting mental health implications.
Could the amount of sugar we consume before birth and during infancy influence our mental health decades later? An experiment rooted in postwar Britain suggests that the effects of our earliest diets may extend far beyond childhood.
During World War II and the years that followed, the United Kingdom strictly rationed sugar, limiting how much families could purchase. When those restrictions ended in September 1953, sugar consumption surged, creating a rare opportunity for scientists to examine how early-life exposure to sugar might shape long-term health.
A study published in
General Psychiatry
found that exposure to rationing during early life was associated with a 17% lower risk of anxiety and a 14% lower risk of depression compared with no exposure. The researchers analyzed data from 66,223 UK Biobank participants born around the policy change, linking the timing of their earliest years to health records later in life.
Sugar rationing offers a natural experiment
Because the availability of other foods remained relatively stable when sugar consumption increased, the end of rationing offered a natural experiment. Researchers could compare people who experienced different periods of restricted sugar availability at the start of life. They estimated exposure using birth dates relative to the policy change, with exposure ranging from before birth only to periods extending through about age two.
Associations of sugar rationing with the risk of anxiety and depression. (A) Anxiety; (B) depression. Credit: Xiuping Dou, Yang Su, Yao Huang, Man He, Bingying Zhang, Xuejin Li, Hualiang Lin, Yin Yang
That approach tracked exposure to a national policy, rather than measuring what individual mothers or children ate. The researchers did not have individual childhood food records, and unmeasured factors, including other aspects of maternal diet, may have influenced the results. The findings therefore cannot establish that lower sugar intake caused the differences in mental health.
Longer rationing, lower anxiety and depression risks
The strongest associations appeared among people exposed to rationing throughout the first 1,000 days after conception, spanning pregnancy and roughly the first two years after birth. Compared with people without early exposure, this group had approximately 24% lower relative risk of anxiety and 21% lower relative risk of depression. Across the analysis, the association generally strengthened with longer exposure to rationing.
For participants exposed throughout those first 1,000 days, diagnoses also appeared later in their health records. The first recorded anxiety diagnosis occurred about two years later, and the first recorded depression diagnosis about four years later, than among participants with no early exposure. These findings concern when diagnoses were first recorded, rather than necessarily when symptoms began.
Early nutrition could potentially influence later mental health through its effects on stress regulation, inflammation, and brain development. The authors drew these possible explanations from previous research, but did not directly test the mechanisms in the UK Biobank analysis. Further studies that measure individual diets and examine other populations will help clarify how dietary conditions during pregnancy and infancy relate to mental health across the life course, and what that relationship could mean for public health.
Reference: “Sugar restriction during the first 1000 days after conception and its association with decreased risk of anxiety and depression” by Xiuping Dou, Yang Su, Yao Huang, Man He, Bingying Zhang, Xuejin Li, Hualiang Lin and Yin Yang, 7 July 2026,
General Psychiatry

title: Animal vs. Plant Protein: New Study Reveals Unexpected Testosterone Differences
content:
New research suggests that different dietary proteins may have distinct relationships with testosterone and hormone-binding proteins. Credit: Shutterstock
An observational study of middle-aged men links animal protein to lower testosterone and plant protein to higher levels, but the differences are small, and their health effects remain unclear.
A protein-rich meal gives the body amino acids, the building blocks it needs to make and repair tissues, including muscle. Testosterone helps regulate muscle growth and also supports bones and sexual function. Food provides essential materials, while hormones help direct what the body does with them.
That connection makes diet a reasonable place to look when studying testosterone, yet relatively few studies have examined its relationship with protein intake.
Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland found that men who consumed more animal protein tended to have lower total testosterone levels in their blood. Those who consumed more plant protein tended to have higher levels. The findings do not mean that higher testosterone is necessarily healthier or that one protein source improves hormone function.
Dairy and meat show different hormone links
The research, published in the
International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition
, included 2,546 men aged 42 to 60 living in eastern Finland. It drew on the university’s ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study. Researchers assessed the men’s diets using four-day food records collected between 1984 and 1989 and measured total testosterone in blood samples. They also measured sex hormone-binding globulin, or SHBG, a protein that binds to sex hormones and influences total testosterone concentrations in the blood.
Looking at individual foods revealed a distinction that the broad category of animal protein could obscure. Higher dairy protein intake was associated with lower total testosterone and SHBG levels. Meat protein intake was associated with lower SHBG, but it had no association with total testosterone. Among plant foods, higher protein intake from vegetables and sources other than cereal products was associated with higher total testosterone.
To compare the differences, the researchers divided the men into four groups according to their protein intake. Those in the highest animal protein group had total testosterone concentrations averaging 1.2 nanomoles per liter (nmol/L) below those in the lowest group. For plant protein, the highest intake group averaged 1.1 nmol/L above the lowest group. SHBG showed similar opposing associations with animal and plant protein intake.
“Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health,” says Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.
Diet’s role in testosterone remains uncertain
Age, excess weight, and lifestyle can influence testosterone levels. The analyses accounted for the men’s age and body mass index, along with several other dietary, lifestyle, and health factors. Even with those adjustments, other aspects of their diets or metabolic factors could help explain the associations.
Because the study was cross-sectional, it cannot establish that eating particular proteins caused the hormone differences. It also cannot determine whether consuming different protein sources affects how much testosterone the body produces or how the hormone acts in the body.

title: Scientists Unlock a Hidden Superconducting Power Inside a Strange Quantum Material
content:
The quantum material tantalum disulfide has paradoxical properties: it consists of layers, one of which becomes superconducting upon cooling while the other acts as an insulator. Under pressure, this interplay changes – and the material becomes superconducting at temperatures roughly three times higher. Credit: Studio HübnerBraun
Researchers have discovered how pressure can unlock hidden superconducting properties in a complex quantum material.
Applying intense pressure to an unusual quantum material can transform how it conducts electricity, allowing superconductivity to spread throughout its three-dimensional structure at temperatures roughly three times higher than normal. Researchers also found a sevenfold increase in the number of electrons participating in superconductivity.
The discovery comes from a team led by Zurab Guguchia at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland. Their findings, published in
Nature Communications
, provide new insight into how superconductivity might be strengthened and eventually achieved under more practical conditions.
A Quantum Material With Opposing Properties
Tantalum disulfide has a simple chemical composition but a remarkably complex electronic structure. It consists of extremely thin atomic layers that behave differently as temperatures fall.
“Its chemical formula sounds very simple: for every tantalum atom there are two sulfur atoms,” says Guguchia. “But inside it is an enormously complex material with almost paradoxical properties.”
When produced in a particular way, the material contains alternating layers with two distinct atomic arrangements. Both conduct electricity at higher temperatures, but cooling causes one to become an insulator while the other becomes superconducting, carrying current without electrical resistance. “This means that the electronic properties of these two layers behave in completely opposite ways,” Guguchia explains.
When the Entire Crystal Becomes Superconducting
Initially, superconductivity remains confined to individual conducting layers because the insulating layers obstruct electron movement between them. But cooling the material to just over 1 kelvin (about −458°F) produces a dramatic change.
“Suddenly the entire material becomes superconducting, so the insulating layers also become conductive and take part in superconductivity,” Guguchia says. Instead of remaining restricted to separate planes, superconductivity extends throughout the crystal in three dimensions.
Scientists knew that applying pressure could raise the temperature at which this transition occurs, but the underlying mechanisms were unclear. The PSI team investigated how compression affects the material’s electrons and the interactions between its layers.
Zurab Guguchia is an experimental solid-state physicist specializing in muon spin rotation and magnetotransport under extreme conditions. He leads a research group focused on discovering and controlling competing quantum phases – superconductivity, magnetism, and charge ordering – using parameters such as pressure, tension, and strong magnetic fields. In 2026, he received the ICSM2026 International Career (Lifetime) Achievement Award on Superconductivity for his outstanding work on novel superconducting materials. Credit: Paul Scherrer Institute PSI/Markus Fischer
How Pressure Strengthens Superconductivity
The researchers subjected tantalum disulfide to pressures several hundred times greater than those inside a typical car tire. Compression brought the superconducting layers closer together, reducing the disruptive effect of the insulating layers. It also allowed previously localized electrons within the insulating layers to participate in superconductivity.
“Due to these effects, high pressure causes tantalum disulfide to become superconducting in all three dimensions at temperatures approximately three times higher.” Measurements also revealed a sevenfold increase in the number of electrons participating in superconductivity.
“So, pressure not only raises the temperature at which superconductivity can occur, but also changes the very nature of the superconducting state,” the researcher explained. “It alters the way electrons pair up and move together through the material, resulting in a more robust form of superconductivity.”
Using Muons to Investigate Electron Behavior
To investigate these changes, the team used muon spin spectroscopy, a technique that detects magnetic conditions inside materials. Muons are elementary particles similar to electrons but approximately 200 times heavier. Although they survive for only a few millionths of a second, their sensitivity to local magnetic fields makes them especially useful for studying superconductors.
“Since muons are exceptionally sensitive probes for magnetic and superconducting properties, we can gain unique insights into quantum materials here at PSI,” Guguchia says.
PSI operates the Swiss Muon Source SμS, the world’s most powerful muon source. By combining muon measurements with other techniques, the researchers examined how pressure changes electron behavior at extremely low temperatures.
Toward Superconductors That Work at Higher Temperatures
Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, eliminating conduction losses and associated waste heat. However, the extreme cooling requirements of most superconducting materials have limited their applications. They are currently used in specialized systems, including the powerful magnets at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider.
“Currently, research is being conducted worldwide on novel, unconventional superconductors that exhibit robust superconductivity even at higher temperatures or in strong external magnetic fields,” Guguchia says.
Although tantalum disulfide still requires extremely low temperatures, the findings demonstrate how pressure can alter electron pairing and strengthen superconductivity. These insights could help researchers develop materials that operate closer to room temperature and under ordinary atmospheric pressure.
“By investigating important quantum materials, we want to uncover the fundamental mechanisms underlying superconductivity,” Guguchia says. “This will allow us to find ways to optimize the temperatures at which superconductivity occurs.”
More Powerful Experiments Ahead
Future experiments at PSI could provide even more detailed measurements. Through the planned IMPACT project (IMPACT stands for: Isotope and Muon Production using Advanced Cyclotron and Target technologies), the institute expects to develop muon beams hundreds of times more powerful than those currently available. Together with the Muoniverse research initiative, the upgrade will expand opportunities to investigate superconducting quantum materials.
“We are already looking forward to the new perspectives these two developments will offer,” Guguchia concludes. “Especially for work on superconducting quantum materials, this opens up unimagined experimental possibilities.”
Reference: “Competing quantum orders in 6R-TaS2 revealed by pressure” by V. Sazgari, J. N. Graham, S. S. Islam, A. Achari, P. Král, O. Gerguri, J. N. Tangermann, J. A. Krieger, H. Gopakumar, G. Simutis, M. Janoschek, M. Bartkowiak, J.-X. Yin, R. Khasanov, H. Luetkens, F. O. von Rohr, R. R. Nair and Z. Guguchia, 30 April 2026,
Nature Communications

title: RadianX secures $9 million and starts a dedicated perovskite module production line
content:
RadianX secures $9 million and starts a dedicated perovskite module production line
, a California-based perovskite module developer formerly known as California Perovskite Technology, has announced $9 million in combined venture and project financing to scale production of its modules. The seed round was co-led by SOSV and Twynam, with participation from One Small Planet, Sahsen Ventures, Avila VC, California Innovation Fund, quantumEDGE, Riceberg Ventures and Alumni Ventures.
As part of the package, Pacific Union Technology Precision Manufacturing (PUT), a publicly listed precision components manufacturer, will fund a dedicated production line to support commercial-volume output. RadianX describes it as its first automated 6 MW line, which it plans to use as a blueprint for larger facilities.
RadianX targets “edge energy” applications such as sensors, wearables, connected devices and Physical AI. The company says its modules generate power in low and indoor light, which can help devices run longer, use smaller batteries and, in some cases, avoid battery replacement. The modules are as thin as 0.7 mm and can be integrated into the surfaces of existing products, the company says. It offers a rigid glass module (AlphaGlass) and a semitransparent version (AlphaVis), and is developing a flexible one (AlphaFlex).
The company says its modules have been certified by TÜV in all three categories of IEC TS 63163, a specification for photovoltaic modules used in consumer products, including Category 3 for products with high outdoor exposure. It also reports certified efficiency at cell, panel and full-module scale, including 22.33% on a 1.2 m x 0.6 m module, and says the modules passed lead-release testing under REACH and comply with RoHS. RadianX adds that it is working with NGK on pairing its modules with NGK’s EnerCera batteries in wireless asset trackers.

title: Fill factor retention helps perovskite mini-module reach certified 23.9% efficiency
content:
Fill factor retention helps perovskite mini-module reach certified 23.9% efficiency
Researchers from
Microquanta Semiconductor
, Zhejiang University, China Three Gorges Renewable, the Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics and the Zhejiang Provincial Key Laboratory of Optoelectronic Functional Materials and Devices have analyzed why perovskite solar cells lose efficiency as they grow from lab-scale devices to modules, and report a processing approach aimed at limiting that loss.
The team compared how different device parameters contribute to the efficiency drop across a range of perovskite technologies, and identified fill factor as a major contributor. They then broke the fill factor deficit down into voltage-related, diode-non-ideality and transport-related contributions. To preserve the fill factor, the researchers used a cryo-controlled processing step that regulates the evolution of an intermediate phase during crystallization. The team says the benefit comes mainly from reduced diode non-ideality, with the other contributions being smaller, and that the advantage increases with device size.
A mini-module with a 19.48 cm² aperture area reached a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9%, with a fill factor of 83.3%. The researchers also say the same fill factor limitation governs performance decay during operation, which links efficiency retention during scale-up with long-term stability.

国家能源局四川监管办公室原党组书记、监管专员何淑兰，因涉嫌严重违纪违法，于2026年10月13日被中央纪委国家监委驻国家发展改革委纪检监察组立案纪律审查，并由四川省监察委员会同步开展监察调查。该案由中央纪委国家监委派驻机构与地方纪委监委联合办理，体现了对能源监管领域权力运行监督的持续强化。何淑兰曾长期在能源监管系统任职，其接受审查调查反映出当前反腐败斗争向重点领域、关键岗位纵深推进的态势。此次通报系官方权威发布，案件正在依规依纪依法办理中。（198字）
2026年9月8日，中央纪委国家监委通报对应急管理部原党委书记、部长王祥喜的审查调查结果。经查，王祥喜丧失理想信念，背离初心使命，严重违反党的多项纪律：违规收受礼金、接受可能影响公正执行公务的宴请，违规参与公款宴请；在干部选拔任用中为他人谋利；利用职权为特定关系人经营活动及他人在工程项目承揽、职务晋升等方面谋取利益，非法收受巨额财物。其行为构成严重职务违法并涉嫌受贿犯罪，且在党的十八大后持续不收敛、不收手，性质恶劣、影响严重。依据相关规定，决定给予其开除党籍、开除公职处分，终止其党的二十大代表资格，收缴违纪违法所得，并将其涉嫌犯罪问题移送检察机关依法审查起诉。
国家能源局四川监管办公室原党组书记、监管专员马军杰因涉嫌严重违纪违法，正接受中央纪委国家监委驻国家发展改革委纪检监察组的纪律审查，以及四川省监察委员会的监察调查。该案件由中央纪委国家监委驻国家发展改革委纪检监察组与四川省纪委监委联合通报，表明其问题线索涉及党的纪律和国家监察双重范畴。马军杰曾长期在能源监管系统担任重要领导职务，其被查反映出能源监管领域反腐败工作的持续深化。目前调查仍在进行中，尚未公布具体违纪违法事实及情节。此次审查调查属于中央纪委国家监委统筹部署下对垂直管理单位领导干部开展的常规监督执纪行动，体现了对公权力运行全过程监督的强化。
晋中市能源局党组成员、副局长王爱青因涉嫌严重违纪违法，于2026年8月20日被山西省纪委监委网站通报，正接受晋中市纪委监委的纪律审查和监察调查。王爱青长期在晋中能源系统任职，担任副局长期间分管煤炭生产技术、油气、发展规划、节能与科技装备等核心业务领域，职权覆盖能源管理关键环节。公开信息显示，其近年多次出席能源转型、新能源基础设施建设等重要发布会并开展实地督导，活跃于地方能源工作一线。此次被查，反映出能源领域作为资金与资源密集型行业，廉政风险持续受到关注。目前案件正在进一步审查中。
国网黑龙江省电力有限公司原党委书记、董事长鲁海威因涉嫌严重违纪违法，于2026年6月起接受中央纪委国家监委驻国家电网有限公司纪检监察组的纪律审查，以及黑龙江省监察委员会的监察调查。鲁海威曾长期在电力系统任职，历任吉林、辽宁、黑龙江三省电力公司多项重要职务，系第十四届全国人大代表，曾获国务院特殊津贴及辽宁省劳动模范称号。此次调查由央企纪检监察机构与地方监委协同开展，体现对能源领域关键岗位领导干部监督执纪的持续深化。目前其职务已由他人接替，相关工作正有序推进。
国家能源集团广西电力有限公司原党委书记、董事长刘宏荣因涉嫌严重违纪违法，于2026年6月1日被正式通报接受纪律审查和监察调查。此次调查由中央纪委国家监委驻国家能源集团纪检监察组与广西壮族自治区监察委员会联合开展，体现“央企派驻机构+地方监委”的协同办案机制。刘宏荣长期在能源系统工作，历任武警水电部队、国电云南及广西分公司、神华广西分公司等多个重要岗位，最终担任国家能源集团广西电力有限公司主要负责人。其被查是当前能源领域持续深化反腐败斗争的又一典型案例，亦与近期多名能源央企高管接连落马的反腐态势相呼应。
4月17日，据中央纪委国家监委驻国家电网有限公司纪检监察组消息：国网江西省电力有限公司原党委副书记、副总经理、工会主席王迪卿涉嫌严重违纪违法，目前正接受中央纪委国家监委驻国家电网有限公司纪检监察组纪律审查和监察调查。
中央纪委国家监委网站12月28日消息，据山西省纪委监委消息：日前，经山西省委批准，山西省纪委监委对中条山有色金属集团有限公司原党委书记、董事长王树琪严重违纪违法问题进行立案审查调查。
据安徽省纪委监委12月22日消息，日前，经中共安徽省委批准，安徽省纪委监委对宿州市委原副书记、市政府原市长王启荣严重违纪违法问题进行了立案审查调查。
12月19日，中国大唐集团有限公司党组书记、董事长吕军，董事、总经理、党组副书记李向良在呼和浩特拜会内蒙古自治区党委书记王伟中，自治区党委副书记、自治区人民政府主席包钢。吕军感谢自治区党委和政府对中国大唐的支持和帮助，并介绍了集团公司在内蒙古的产业布局和项目建设情况。内蒙古自治区、中国大唐相关部门及企业负责人参加会谈。

content:
省政府新闻办“《‘绿动渤海’行动方案(2026—2030年)河北篇》政策解读新闻发布会”新闻发布会文字实录
10月29日上午，河北省人民政府新闻办公室举行“《‘绿动渤海’行动方案(2026—2030年)河北篇》政策解读”新闻发布会。河北海事局党组成员、副局长李义良介绍解读《“绿动渤海”行动方案(2026—2030年)河北篇》相关内容;河北省交通运输厅港航处处长高建伟，中国人民银行河北省分行金融研究处处长赵天奕，河北省发展改革委能源局新能源处三级调研员侯晓丽，河北海事局秦皇岛海上溢油应急反应中心主任王晓磊共同回答大家关心的问题。发布会由河北省委宣传部(省政府新闻办)新闻发布处二级调研员吴志同主持。实录如下：
河北省委宣传部(省政府新闻办)新闻发布处二级调研员吴志同：
女士们、先生们，记者朋友们：
大家上午好!欢迎出席河北省人民政府新闻办公室新闻发布会。
为贯彻落实省委、省政府和交通运输部关于绿色低碳发展要求，近日，河北海事局会同省交通运输厅、省发展改革委等10部门印发了《“绿动渤海”行动方案(2026—2030年)河北篇》，为了方便大家更好地了解相关政策，今天我们邀请到河北海事局党组成员、副局长李义良先生，请他介绍解读《“绿动渤海”行动方案(2026—2030年)河北篇》相关内容;同时，我们还邀请到河北省交通运输厅港航处处长高建伟先生，中国人民银行河北省分行金融研究处处长赵天奕女士，河北省发展改革委能源局新能源处三级调研员侯晓丽女士，河北海事局秦皇岛海上溢油应急反应中心主任王晓磊先生，他们将共同回答大家关心的问题。
首先，请李义良先生作介绍，有请。
河北海事局党组成员、副局长李义良：
各位记者朋友，女士们、先生们：
很高兴在此和大家见面。首先，感谢各位长期以来对河北海事工作的关注与支持。
习近平总书记高度重视海洋生态环境保护，强调“要高度重视海洋生态文明建设，加强海洋环境污染防治，保护海洋生物多样性，实现海洋资源有序开发利用，为子孙后代留下一片碧海蓝天”，为我们推动海洋生态保护和海洋产业绿色转型指明了方向、提供了根本遵循。交通运输部就国家“十五五”规划中完善现代化综合交通运输体系这一重大任务，作出了“一网四化”的具体部署，明确提出推动交通运输绿色化转型的工作要求。今年5月19日，交通运输部海事局印发《“绿动渤海”行动方案(2026—2030年)》，部署实施“绿动渤海”行动，是统筹推进降碳、减污、扩绿、增长，服务国家“双碳”战略的重大举措。河北秦皇岛、唐山、沧州三大港口是京津冀核心出海门户，在环渤海绿色发展格局中地位重要、责任重大。为深入贯彻习近平生态文明思想，积极稳妥推进碳达峰碳中和，在省委、省政府坚强领导下，河北海事局会同省发展改革委、省交通运输厅、省生态环境厅等部门，系统梳理我省港航绿色发展现状，深入调研、广泛座谈、反复论证，研究制定了《“绿动渤海”行动方案(2026—2030年)河北篇》(以下简称《行动方案》)，经省政府审定同意后正式印发实施。
《行动方案》起草过程中，我们始终践行“三个坚持”：
坚持对标对表、服务大局。紧密衔接国家“双碳”战略、交通运输领域绿色低碳发展部署，将国家战略转化为河北港航、海洋产业可操作、可落地的具体举措，确保中央部署和部、省要求在我省不折不扣落地见效。
坚持立足省情、突出特色。充分发挥河北港口群规模优势、临港产业基础优势和环渤海区位优势，聚焦老旧船舶占比偏高、清洁能源供给不足、岸电使用率不高等突出问题，在船舶绿色转型、港口低碳建设、海上风光电融合等领域精准发力，走出一条具有河北特色的绿色发展之路。
坚持协同联动、系统治理。统筹港口航运、临港产业、海洋产业、生态保护全链条，深化跨区域、跨部门协同，推动津冀及环渤海省市资源共享、航线共建、应急联动，形成陆海统筹、区域联动、多方参与的绿色发展合力。
《行动方案》围绕“加快航运绿色低碳转型、推进港口低碳智能建设、赋能临港绿色产业升级、强化全域污染协同防治、健全要素支撑保障机制”五大板块，提出20项具体任务，着力打造绿色港航示范区。下面，我从五个方面作简要解读。
第一，加快航运绿色低碳转型，优化运输结构体系。方案从船舶、燃料、运输组织、航线网络四个维度系统推进：一是推动船舶绿色低碳转型，加快老旧营运船舶报废更新，引导新建改造船舶应用新能源清洁能源，聚焦沿海短途货船、港作拖轮、旅游船艇推广电池动力等清洁动力，支持秦皇岛山船重工等企业强化绿色船舶研发制造。二是推进船舶绿色燃料应用，研究推进港口绿色燃料加注基础设施建设，支持曹妃甸LNG码头加注改造等绿色燃料加注产业发展，有序落地绿色燃料加注示范项目。三是优化交通运输组织模式，纵深推进“公转铁”“公转水”，深入实施多式联运。提升港口作业效率、减少船舶待港时间，建立绿色船舶库，实行绿色船舶“一船一策”、绿色航线“一线一策”、绿色走廊“一廊一策”，推广船舶“四直”绿通和“八优”快线模式。四是打造绿色示范航线网络，推动唐山港至山东博兴港、滨州港等绿色航线建设，探索构建国际绿色航运走廊。
第二，推进港口低碳智能建设，夯实绿色发展根基。方案提出：一是深化港口清洁能源使用，有序推动港口作业装备新能源替代，全面推进岸电设施提档升级，推动组建渤海“岸电使用绿色联盟”，大力推进港口“风光储充”一体化项目建设。二是加快绿色低碳港口创建，支持建设“近零碳港区”“零碳码头”“零碳运输线路试点”，聚焦黄骅港煤炭港区打造近零碳港区，到2030
年专业化散货码头全部建成星级绿色港口。三是提升港口智慧绿色运营水平，依托数智化技术升级运营管控体系，强化能耗排放实时监测，推进港区绿化美化和生态缓冲带建设，实现港口生产与生态保护协同发展。
第三，赋能海洋产业绿色升级，培育低碳发展动能。方案明确：一是有序推进海上风电光伏项目建设，加快秦皇岛、唐山、沧州海上清洁能源项目建设，推进海上风电与海洋石油、海洋牧场、海洋算力融合发展，结合唐秦负荷中心需求实施“海上风电+绿电直连”实施项目。二是加快推动油田绿色发展，鼓励绿电就近接入油田生产系统，推动秦皇岛—曹妃甸油田群岸电扩容，支持秦皇岛
油田建成“低碳零碳作业区”。三是大力发展新能源船舶、高端海工装备等绿色制造产业，谋划实施秦皇岛无人船制造、智能港口设备制造等项目，有序布局海水制氢等前沿产业。
第四，强化全域污染协同防治，提升海洋生态环境。方案从四个方面强化治理：一是从严管控船舶污染排放，综合运用卫星遥感、无人机巡查等科技手段构建立体化监管体系，严格船舶排放控制区监管，常态化开展燃油硫含量和尾气处理装置检查。二是系统提升港口污染治理水平，严格落实环保设施“三同时”制度，完善船舶污染物接收转运处置闭环管控，打造煤炭码头“无废港口”示范港，到2030年煤炭本质抑尘技术全面应用，干散货码头绿色化水平国际领先。三是提升海上污染应急能力，充分发挥环渤海区域海上污染应急协同机制作用，加强溢油应急队伍建设，常态化开展应急演练与技能比武。四是深化海洋生态环境风险防范，动态排查涉海环境风险隐患，编制海湾生态环境风险“一湾一图”，巩固提升秦皇岛湾等美丽海湾建设成效，与天津市协同加强入海排污口监管，促进津冀区域海洋环境规范管理水平共同提升。
第五，健全要素支撑保障机制，夯实绿色发展根基。方案从法规、金融、体系、人才、数智、履约六个方面强化保障：一是完善法规政策标准体系，修订完善《河北省防治船舶污染海洋环境管理办法》等法规，推动水运领域绿色低碳标准修订和制定。二是发挥蓝色金融支撑作用，创新蓝色信贷产品，探索海域使用权、海洋碳汇等非传统抵押品信贷模式，推广EOD模式，鼓励研发清洁能源船舶专项保险。三是推动降碳减污动态监测和科学评价体系建设，探索建立港航和海洋产业碳排放统计核算评价体系。四是加强人才队伍建设，深化校企合作产教融合，布局双燃料船舶船员培养见习点。五是提升数智化管控能力，加快智慧航道、智慧交管建设，在秦皇岛、沧州开展低能见度通航技术研究应用，建设海上搜救智能化辅助决策系统。六是强化国际海事履约与涉外航运治理，严格落实国际公约要求，提升河北港口国际化服务能力和对外开放水平。
方案明确要求各地各部门在省委、省政府统一领导下压实工作责任、强化协同联动，加强科研投入破解技术瓶颈，深化区域“政产学研用”协同，组建产业联盟、共建合作平台，加强与环渤海省市协同联动，凝聚起全社会共同推动绿色发展的强大合力。
各位媒体朋友，“绿动渤海”行动河北篇是一项助力国家“双碳”战略落地、筑牢渤海生态安全屏障、赋能河北港航和海洋产业高质量发展的系统性、战略性工程。诚挚希望社会各界持续关注和支持，为服务全国绿色低碳发展大局，加快建设经济强省、美丽河北作出更大贡献!

感谢记者朋友的提问。渤海是河北重要的海洋能源资源战略接续区，也是“绿动渤海”绿色航运转型的清洁能源基座。结合我省即将印发的可再生能源发展“十五五”规划总体部署，《行动方案》将海上新能源开发纳入绿色航运转型总体框架，围绕“陆海统筹、风光并举、融合发展、安全高效”的总体思路，对未来五年海上新能源开发与港航绿色低碳转型深度融合作出系统安排。
一是海上风电光伏规模化推进。在秦皇岛、唐山、沧州沿海三市科学布局，有序推进海上风电、海上光伏项目建设。海上风电方面，山海关海上风电一期、河北建投唐山海上风电、唐山顺桓海上风电等项目梯次推进;海上光伏方面，秦皇岛市180万千瓦海上光伏示范试点项目、秦皇岛市200万千瓦“风光同场”海上光伏项目加快实施。二是探索海上新能源绿电直连实现新突破。落实单用户、多用户绿电直连配套政策，建立“随报随批”绿色审批通道，结合唐山、秦皇岛负荷中心需求，指导沿海三市探索实施“海上风电+绿电直连”示范，推动海上绿电通过专用线路向钢铁、化工等临港大工业点对点供电，助力重点产品满足出口碳足迹要求，把海上绿电优势切实转化为临港产业绿色竞争优势。三是探索新能源与海洋多元融合发展。有序推动海上风电、海上光伏与海洋牧场、海洋算力、海水淡化、海水制氢、海上油田等集成融合，培育海洋绿色新兴产业，形成多能互补、立体开发、融合发展的海洋能源利用新格局。
下一步，我委将按照《行动方案》部署，进一步加强与国家及省直有关部门的沟通对接，统筹海域空间、生态保护、航运安全等多重因素，有序推进海上新能源项目前期工作与工程建设，积极谋划储备后续项目，持续扩大海上清洁能源供给，为绿色航运、港口运营和临港产业提供稳定清洁电力保障，为加快建设经济强省、美丽河北贡献能源力量。谢谢。
二、河北日报：《行动方案》提出，到2030年专业化散货码头全部建成星级绿色港口。请问“十四五”以来，我省绿色港口建设取得了哪些成效?“十五五”期间，省交通运输厅将如何抓好《行动方案》的落实?
河北省交通运输厅港航处处长高建伟：
感谢这位记者的提问。近年来，我厅深入学习贯彻习近平生态文明思想，按照省委、省政府和交通运输部部署要求，全力抓好港口污染防治、岸电建设使用、运输结构调整等工作，港口绿色发展保持全国领先。一是污染防治水平行业领先。全面推广煤炭本质抑尘技术，秦皇岛港、黄骅港实现煤炭全流程自动化作业，粉尘防治技术全国领先;建成世界最大规模封闭式条形仓，全省专业化干散货堆场实现防风抑尘设施全覆盖。二是岸电使用全国领先。全省港口建成岸电设施153套，覆盖泊位179个，5万吨级以上专业化泊位岸电覆盖率100%;2025年岸电供电量1871.6万度、同比增长15.6%，黄骅港煤炭港区岸电使用率100%、用电量居全国干散货港区首位。三是绿色疏港比例居全国前列。全省已形成大宗货物中长距离采用铁路水路运输、短距离采用封闭式皮带廊道和新能源车辆运输的集疏港体系，2025年大宗货物绿色疏港比例达95%以上，高于国家要求15个百分点。四是绿色示范创建走在前列。秦皇岛港获评全国首家5星级“绿色港区”，唐山港集团港企联动大宗货物零碳运输线路获评交通运输部零碳试点项目，黄骅港煤三期码头入选全国首批“零碳港口”试点。
