三、光明网：蓝色金融是助力海洋产业转型升级与海洋生态保护的金融抓手。请问中国人民银行河北省分行在推动蓝色金融标准试用与“绿动渤海”行动衔接方面，主要开展了哪些工作，取得了怎样的成效?
中国人民银行河北省分行金融研究处处长赵天奕：
蓝色金融作为绿色金融在海洋领域的重要延伸和实践拓展，是服务国家海洋强国战略、助力海洋产业转型升级与海洋生态保护修复的关键抓手。中国人民银行河北省分行立足河北海洋产业发展格局，以“一套标准、五大领域、三地试用”的框架推动蓝色金融标准试用与“绿动渤海”行动融合发展，以高质量蓝色金融服务护航河北向海图强。一是制定了一套蓝色金融试用标准，明确五大重点支持领域。按照中国人民银行总行蓝色金融标准试用工作要求，中国人民银行河北省分行牵头印发《河北省蓝色金融标准试用工作指引》，重点满足海洋节能降碳、海洋资源循环利用、海洋清洁能源、海洋生态保护修复、海洋基础设施绿色升级等五大领域的海洋产业融资需求，并鼓励拓展海洋环境保护、海洋绿色服务与绿色贸易相关金融服务。二是引导省内秦皇岛、唐山、沧州沿海三地开展蓝色金融标准试用，加大蓝色信贷投放力度。自标准试用以来，省内秦皇岛、唐山、沧州沿海三地符合蓝色金融标准的蓝色信贷余额实现较快增长，蓝色信贷加权平均利率显著低于各项贷款平均利率水平。沿海三地立足资源禀赋差异，形成了秦皇岛聚焦海洋文旅、唐山主攻海洋清洁能源、沧州深耕海盐化工的差异化蓝色信贷发展格局。三是拓宽蓝色金融支持场景，推动蓝色金融标准试用与“绿动渤海”行动融合发展。一方面，“绿动渤海”行动为蓝色金融标准落地提供丰富的应用场景与优质项目储备，蓝色金融标准试用能够鼓励和引导金融机构加大对绿色船舶建造、港口岸电升级与新能源替代等领域的资金支持。另一方面，“绿动渤海”行动重点任务均属蓝色金融重点支持范畴，蓝色金融能够满足“绿动渤海”行动项目全周期资金需求。
下一步，中国人民银行河北省分行将联合河北海事局共建蓝色金融项目库，将“绿动渤海”重点项目纳入蓝色金融支持范围;将蓝色金融纳入绿色金融评估考核体系，发挥碳减排支持工具、支农支小再贷款等货币政策工具作用，鼓励和引导金融机构结合绿动渤海行动创新更多蓝色金融产品;将海事监管数据与金融机构贷前尽调、贷中审查、贷后风险管理等业务深度融合，为金融机构全链条风险管控提供支撑。
四、香港商报：河北海事局助力河北省港航和海洋产业绿色低碳发展有哪些举措?

title: 美国中期选举落幕, 光伏迎来预期重估？-索比光伏网
content:
11月5日，A股光伏板块集体走强，多只龙头个股大幅上涨。据悉，本轮行情最核心的外部因素是刚刚落幕的美国中期选举：民主党成功拿下参议院、众议院两院控制权，市场对于美国清洁能源补贴政策被大幅削减的担忧快速降温。
什么是美国中期选举：美国总统每届任期4年，在总统任期到一半的时候会举行中期选举，选举对象是全部众议院席位、约1/3参议院席位，同时还有部分州长、地方公职。中期选举不选总统，但会直接决定国会两院由哪个政党掌控。总统可以提出法案，但法案想要落地、预算想要通过，都需要国会配合。如果在野党掌控国会，就容易掣肘总统的政策，甚至削减、冻结对应项目预算，这也是资本市场非常重视中期选举结果的核心原因。
在此之前，IRA《通胀削减法案》一直是美国光伏市场最重要的政策基石。法案中的ITC光伏投资税收抵免、储能税收优惠、本土制造补贴，支撑了美国近几年光伏、储能装机的快速扩张。市场长期存在一个巨大顾虑：如果共和党掌控国会，将会推动缩减甚至废除IRA里面的绿色补贴条款，光伏项目补贴提前到期、美国装机预期下调，这一风险长期压制光伏板块估值，尤其是面向海外出口的组件、逆变器企业股价。
两党能源路线差异十分清晰。共和党更偏向传统化石能源，多次提出提案压缩新能源补贴预算；而民主党是IRA法案的主导方，倾向维持清洁能源激励政策、推进电网改造、简化新能源项目审批流程。本次选举结果落地，意味着IRA核心补贴框架被国会立法层面砍掉的尾部风险大幅消除，美国光伏开发商、电站运营商的长期投资预期得以稳定。补贴确定性提升之后，地面电站、工商业分布式光伏更容易谈妥长期电力采购协议（PPA），项目融资难度下降，机构开始上调美国未来几年光伏装机指引。
美国市场户用光伏、大型地面电站、配套储能需求预期修复，直接利好具备美国市场交付、合规能力的出口型企业；而以国内供应链为主、不直接面向美国市场的环节，更多是跟随板块情绪联动，业绩兑现的直接影响偏弱。
但需要理性区分：这一轮上涨是可能是政策预期修复驱动的反弹，不意味着行业基本面反转。
首先，IRA本身还有贸易、本土化配套的门槛，国内企业进入美国市场依然要面对相关合规限制，政策稳定不等于订单立刻爆发；同时也要看到，即便民主党掌控国会，党内也存在不同声音，后续IRA补贴细则调整、资金发放节奏依然存在变数；
其次，当前全球光伏产能过剩的格局没有根本改变，硅料、组件价格依旧偏低，多数制造企业盈利压力还在，后续行情能不能持续，需要持续跟踪组件报价、美国项目落地进度、海外订单数据。
短期看，中期选举结果消除了一个最大的海外利空变量；中长期看，行业走势最终还是要看供需出清节奏、毛利率修复和海内外装机真实落地情况。

title: SSE marks two years of construction for the Eastern Green Link 2
content:
SSE marks two years of construction for the Eastern Green Link 2 TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
SSE marks two years of construction for the Eastern Green Link 2
SSE has announced a major milestone for the Eastern Green Link 2 (EGL2)
project, marking two years since construction began on what is set to become
the UK's largest electricity transmission project.
A joint venture between SSEN Transmission and National Grid Electricity
Transmission, the £4.3 billion project will deliver a 505 km electricity
superhighway linking Peterhead with Drax.
The project will also feature the UK's largest subsea high-voltage direct
current (HVDC) cable. Once complete, EGL2 will be capable of transporting
up to 2 GW of electricity, helping to strengthen the UK's energy network
and support the integration of renewable generation.
According to SSE, significant progress has been made at the Yorkshire site,
where construction of permanent buildings is now underway. The steel frame
for the first converter building has been completed, alongside the first
alternating current hall. Construction of both transformer buildings has
also been completed.
Installation of the onshore underground cable is continuing in Peterhead,
while offshore works remain ongoing. Following the completion of horizontal
directional drilling at Sandford Bay, similar operations are now taking
place at Fraisthorpe.
"From our converter stations in Aberdeenshire and Yorkshire to the
onshore and subsea cable works and the manufacture of specialist equipment,
we're seeing strong progress across the project," said Fionán Doonan,
EGL2 Project Director.

MetOceanWorks has announced that its metocean design basis for EnBW's 1
GW Dreekant
offshore wind farmhas received independent certification from TÜV SÜD.
The company was appointed to the project back in 2025 to develop a 45 year
wind, wave and hydrodynamic hindcast to support the wind farm's design

The design basis was created using measurements collected across the region

the requirements of BSH and IEC standards.
The certified design basis will support the detailed engineering and design

potential changes in seabed levels to support engineering, installation
and project planning activities throughout the project's development.

Ofgem selects preferred bidder for Dogger Bank B transmission assets
Energy regulator Ofgem has announced that, under the Gas and Electricity
Markets Authority's offshore transmission owner regime, Diamond Transmission
Partners has been selected as the preferred bidder for the 1.2 GW Dogger
offshore wind farm.
Dogger Bank B forms part of the wider Dogger Bank Wind Farm development,
located around 130 km off the northeast coast of England. Once fully operational,
the 3.6 GW project is expected to generate enough electricity to power
up to 6 million UK homes annually.
The appointment remains subject to several conditions and approvals required
as the offshore transmission owner.
Under the proposed arrangements, Diamond Transmission Partners will be
required to establish the funding, regulatory and operational frameworks
necessary to provide offshore transmission services for the project.
The company must also put in place a bilateral agreement with the holder
of the co-ordination licence and resolve any additional matters deemed
necessary by the Authority before the appointment can be finalised.

title: Finnish Government outlines offshore wind auction process
政策分类路径: 政策 > 监管落实型政策 > 正外部性 > 可再生能源优惠
政策分类依据: 芬兰政府正式公布海上风电拍卖框架，通过竞争性招标规则支持海上风电项目开发，属可再生能源支持机制
content:
The Finnish government has formally outlined details of its offshore wind
auction framework, identifying four designated areas for potential offshore
wind development and proposing new rules supporting the construction and
decommissioning of projects.
The areas selected for development are Selkämeri länsi (Bothnian Sea West),
Selkämeri itä (Bothnian Sea East), Perämeri etelä (Bothnian Bay South)
and Perämeri pohjoinen (Bothnian Bay North). Perämeri etelä is expected
to be the first area offered for auction, potentially in the first half
of 2027, with the remaining three areas to follow.
With the development zones now identified, a competitive tender process
will be used to select a project developer for each area. Bids will be
evaluated based on both price and qualitative criteria, with each accounting
for half of the overall assessment.
According to the proposal, environmental impact assessments have already
been completed for the designated areas. However, the successful developer
for each zone will be required to undertake more detailed project-specific
studies.
The proposal would introduce additional provisions to Finland's Water Act
covering the construction and decommissioning of offshore wind farms in
the country's exclusive economic zone, including requirements related to
decommissioning security.
Under the proposed framework, the Finnish Supervisory Agency would determine
on a case-by-case basis how much offshore infrastructure must be removed
once a wind farm reaches the end of its operational life.
Developers would also be permitted to build their decommissioning funds
gradually after a project begins commercial operations, reducing upfront
costs and potentially improving access to project financing.
TGS | 4C Finland Analyst Chris Ayres said: "Good to see some momentum
behind these four sites. However, without state aid, thereby requiring
wind farms to be built on highly strained market terms, these projects
are ultimately not yet profitable. In the long-term, this challenge must
be overcome if we are to see steel in Finnish EEZ waters."

title: TSMC Weighs Making Advanced Memory Chips to Capture More AI Spending
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. is considering expanding into the advanced memory chip manufacturing sector, a move that would give the world’s largest chipmaker an even bigger share of the AI hardware supply chain, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The Taiwanese chipmaking giant recently started drawing up plans for making a specific type of advanced memory chips, 3D DRAM, at the request of Nvidia, its biggest customer, the two people said. An intense shortage of memory chips, driven by the AI hardware boom, has sent prices soaring and prompted chip designers such as Nvidia and Apple to look for sources of additional supply. Apple earlier this year hiked prices for its devices, citing rising memory costs. DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory, holds data while a processor uses it. Unlike traditional DRAM, which puts memory cells in a single layer, 3D DRAM stacks layers of cells vertically to fit more memory. Memory chip manufacturing is now dominated by Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology. The trio is also developing 3D DRAM technology, setting up a contest for the next generation of memory manufacturing. It couldn’t be learned when TSMC plans to begin production or how the company intends to secure the manufacturing facilities required. TSMC could opt to build new factories, the two people added. Another avenue it is exploring is acquiring an existing plant and converting it for memory production, the two people with direct knowledge said. Micron is doing something similar: in March, Micron bought a plant from Taiwan’s Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp. for $1.8 billion, with plans to convert the site for advanced memory production. TSMC’s choice of facilities and production scale would shape how quickly it becomes a competitor to established memory suppliers. TSMC has a history of making standard memory chips from the 1990s to the late 2000s. The company was disclosing revenue from memory until the second quarter of 2008. “We don’t comment on market rumors or speculation,” TSMC said in a statement. “TSMC focuses on our core business at all times, which is dedicated [integrated circuit] foundry. Our mission is to be the trusted technology and capacity provider of the global logic [integrated circuit]] industry for years to come,” the statement said. Nvidia didn’t reply to requests for comment. The move into memory chip manufacturing would leave TSMC vulnerable to a notoriously cyclical segment of the global semiconductor industry. Memory shortages in the past have typically spurred a rush to expand production, but frequently demand has declined by the time additional supply can be delivered. That drives down prices and chipmakers’ profit margins. The boom-and-bust pattern could motivate TSMC to hold off on the memory venture, especially if supply increases or demand subsides in the coming quarters. TSMC’s memory initiative is led by Hsu Kuo-chin, a vice president who oversees advanced packaging, the technology that connects multiple chips into one tightly integrated system, the two people said. Hsu previously led Micron’s Taiwan operations, giving him experience in both memory manufacturing and chip integration, according to his company biography. Another complication of TSMC’s memory push is that in 2024 it struck a partnership with SK Hynix to use TSMC’s manufacturing technology for the base chip beneath SK Hynix’s next-generation high-bandwidth memory. HBM stacks several memory chips to supply data quickly to AI processors; the base chip manages the connections. TSMC has been exploring memory technology for years. It has several patents for vertical DRAM designs describing ways to pack more memory into each chip by building storage structures upward. But turning research into reliable, large-scale production could take years, especially when it comes to 3D DRAM. Packing in additional layers increases manufacturing complexity and opportunities for defects. Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron have spent decades refining how to make memory cheaply and consistently.

title: Chesky’s Side Quest
content: Once upon a time, being CEO of a public company was a full-time job. In fact, for most CEOs, it still is—and an exhausting one at that . So it’s a little puzzling to see that a growing number of tech CEOs are embarking on their own side quests, including most recently Airbnb’s Brian Chesky, who has started an AI lab, as Bloomberg reported earlier this year. Airbnb disclosed Thursday, as it reported third-quarter earnings, that it had sold some intellectual property to Chesky’s new venture for $7.1 million in cash. Airbnb also got the right to invest in any future equity financings of the venture and to license “certain” IP of the lab for internal use in Airbnb’s business. (Hopefully, the IP Airbnb will license isn’t the same IP it just sold to the lab.) Get this: It’s not just Chesky who is involved. Airbnb Chief Technology Officer Ahmad Al-Dahle also has equity in the venture and, like Chesky, “performs services” for it. In a securities filing, Airbnb claimed that “their roles with the AI Lab do not change their duties and responsibilities to Airbnb and they continue to devote the time and attention necessary to fulfil those responsibilities.” Hmmm. If an employee of yours told you they had started a part-time job, and it wouldn’t affect what they did for you, wouldn’t you wonder if maybe they didn’t have enough work to do? How on earth can Airbnb say a side quest won’t affect the time Chesky devotes to his CEO role? By definition, having another venture has to at least distract Chesky. Airbnb defended the arrangement by saying a special committee of independent board members approved it. (For more details, see our story .) To be sure, other CEOs have started side ventures. Several years ago, Coinbase’s Brian Armstrong co-founded a healthcare research firm, NewLimit, although his role is as a board member, not CEO, according to its website . Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev co-founded an AI firm, Harmonic , of which he is executive chair. Jack Dorsey for a time was CEO of both Twitter and Block, while Elon Musk more famously runs multiple companies—including SpaceX and Tesla, both of which are public. Chesky’s distraction is nothing compared to Musk’s. But using Elon Musk as the benchmark for anything in corporate governance is silly. The benchmark should be what’s in the interests of shareholders. Chesky has run Airbnb since he co-founded it in 2008. It would be natural that he has become a bit bored—let’s face it, Airbnb is not the most exciting company in the world—and is looking for a new challenge. But if that’s the case, he should step aside as CEO and allow someone with fresh ideas to take over while he pursues his AI dreams. He could become a nonexecutive chair—a win-win! Amazon’s Wonder Jab The timing could have been better. The same day Marc Lore’s food business, Wonder Group, said it had filed confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission to go public, Amazon ended a deal it had offering Prime members the ability to order restaurant meals via Wonder’s Grubhub. Amazon switched to Uber Eats, which is quite the boost for that business. It’s not great news for DoorDash, either. But for Wonder, which bought Grubhub at the start of last year for $650 million, losing Amazon as a distribution partner cannot be good. title: Cyera’s $800 Million Haul Shows Cyber Fever Hasn’t Broken
content: Last week my colleagues Jemima and Valida scooped that Cyera, a five-year-old cloud security startup, was mulling a new fundraise at an eye-popping $20 billion valuation, up from $12 billion in June. Since then, those talks have gotten more serious, I’ve learned. Cyera is indeed planning to raise around $800 million in a round led by Cyberstarts, which wrote the startup’s first seed check in 2021, according to two people with knowledge of the deal. The funding will value Cyera at $20 billion and is expected to close in the coming weeks, the people said, making Cyera one of the most valuable private cybersecurity companies in the world. Cyera sells software that scans customers’ cloud storage, databases and email systems to identify and track sensitive data and automatically flag potential gaps in security. It’s not clear if the valuation includes the new money. The deal talks follow surging revenue at the startup over the past year. Its annual recurring revenue is now in the hundreds of millions, one of the people said. A Cyera spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. The new round shows how highly investors are valuing cybersecurity startups that defend against AI-powered threats. Such startups have also been the target of acquisitions. Late Wednesday, Valida reported Palo Alto Networks has considered a $500 million acquisition of Clutch Security, which develops software that helps companies track passwords and authentication codes used by AI agents. Workday, Okta and Crowdstrike have also acquired startups that manage AI agents’ identities in recent months . Cyera’s new round would be a rare later-stage investment by Cyberstarts, the Israel-based venture capital fund led by Gili Raanan that primarily invests in early-stage companies. Cyberstarts has notched a series of notable returns in recent years. The most significant was Google’s $34 billion March acquisition of Wiz, which Cyberstarts had invested at the seed stage years earlier. When Cyberstarts wrote Cyera’s seed check five years ago, it was for $4.2 million at a $15 million valuation. The firm has also participated in subsequent Cyera rounds. Cyberstarts has helped Cyera in other ways. It played a key role orchestrating Cyera’s $1 billion acquisition earlier this year of the identity security firm Oasis, another Cyberstarts portfolio company, according to one of the people. Cyberstarts managing director Lior Simon sits on the boards of both companies. The white-hot interest in cybersecurity firms shouldn’t come as a surprise to anyone who has been reading the news lately. Ever since Anthropic unveiled its Mythos model this spring, cybersecurity experts have warned that AI would aid hackers’ ability to find new weaknesses in corporate defenses and supercharge the number of public hacks. In recent weeks, those warnings have come to bear, as a string of high-profile vulnerabilities and cyberattacks aided by AI have left companies scrambling. And more than half a dozen cybersecurity executives told me last month that they’re planning to spend more than ever on security software, including a growing list of tools they say are necessary to address AI threats. For that reason alone, we’re likely to see an increase in the pace of cybersecurity deals in the months ahead, both as large incumbents consolidate dominant firms and as younger startups raise large rounds on the back of revenue growth from surging demand. title: Airbnb Founder Chesky Is Self-Funding His New AI Startup
content: Airbnb on Thursday shed new light on a secretive AI startup that founder and CEO Brian Chesky controls, saying the company has reached an agreement that could allow it to invest in the startup and license its technology. Chesky has so far self-funded the AI lab and plans to continue financing it, according to a person with knowledge of his plans. The new details, some of which were disclosed in a securities filing after Airbnb’s quarterly report, involve a startup Chesky has kept in stealth mode for much of the last year as he continues to run the short-term rental site he founded nearly two decades ago. Airbnb Chief Technology Officer Ahmad Al-Dahle, who joined Airbnb in January after running aspects of Meta’s AI organization, has been advising the startup. Chesky has a controlling interest in the startup while Al-Dahle also owns equity in it, the filing said. Chesky, who owns about 10% of Airbnb but controls around a third of the company’s voting power, has a net worth of nearly $12 billion, according to Forbes. The startup has office space, a third person said. The startup has incorporated under the name Kaboodle Labs in San Francisco, according to a California filing, but that name is a placeholder, said the person with knowledge. Chesky’s involvement in the business echoes the moves of other seasoned technology founders who have created their own AI startups over the past year. Last November, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos launched AI engineering and manufacturing startup Prometheus. Former Airtable CEO Howie Liu is running a new AI agent startup called Hyperagent that originally started within Airtable, the database app sold to Bending Spoons in September. But few CEOs of large public companies—with the exception of Tesla’s Elon Musk, Block’s Jack Dorsey and Apple’s Steve Jobs—have managed to run multiple companies at once, and shareholders in these companies have sometimes complained that the CEOs’ attention was spread too thin. Airbnb in the filing said the roles of Chesky and Al-Dahle “do not change their duties and responsibilities to Airbnb, and they continue to devote the time and attention necessary to fulfill those responsibilities.” Though Chesky plans to fund the AI lab with his own capital for now, it’s possible that the intense need for capital for AI startups, either to get access to talent or AI chips, could push it to eventually take outside funding. Startups that train their own models, otherwise known as neolabs, have been raising billions of dollars within just a few years of launching. Bloomberg in June reported that Chesky planned to start a new company. In Thursday’s disclosure, Airbnb also said the new AI lab had acquired certain intellectual property from Airbnb and reimbursed it for certain expenses in exchange for $7.1 million in cash. The nature of the IP couldn’t be learned. Chesky co-founded Airbnb in 2007 with Joe Gebbia and Nathan Blecharczyk. The trio led the company through a period of regulatory pushback, near-shutdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic, a blockbuster initial public offering and then a surge in revenue as travel resumed. When growth slowed in recent years, Chesky pursued a variety of paths to reinvent the company—for example, by offering travel experiences like tours. More recently he hired Al-Dahle to focus on using AI in Airbnb’s operations , including through AI-powered customer service and travel agents. While Airbnb has had a long relationship with OpenAI, Chesky has also advocated for using open-source models to cut costs, saying some like Alibaba’s Qwen can be “ faster and cheaper ” for many queries. Airbnb on Wednesday said it had fine-tuned a small, open-source AI model using Airbnb-specific data, allowing the company to detect potential violations of its pricing and payment transparency policies faster and at a fraction of the cost of larger AI models. Al-Dahle oversaw Meta’s generative AI team, formed in 2023. He left early this year after a series of restructurings of Meta’s AI labs, including one following Meta’s partial acquisition of Scale AI and the appointment of Scale co-founder Alexandr Wang, who co-leads the organization.

title: Nvidia’s Answer to Data Center Backlash: Retrofitting Apollo’s Old Phone Buildings
content: Nvidia is looking for a faster way to get its chips turned on: old telecom company buildings. The chip designer has approached private equity firm Apollo Global Management about creating a network of small AI data centers potentially spanning 20 states across the U.S., using existing buildings of a struggling telecom firm, according to two people with direct knowledge of the effort. Such a project could help Nvidia and its customers find alternatives following Tuesday’s election of U.S. gubernatorial candidates, including in the all-important state of Texas, who have called on moratoriums on new data centers and other regulations. Retrofitting existing buildings with AI servers could help these companies avoid some of the forthcoming red tape. The telecom-facility project took on greater urgency in recent weeks, as Nvidia pursued a plan to repurpose the assets of Brightspeed, an Apollo-owned broadband internet service provider that is reportedly nearing bankruptcy, the people said. Brightspeed operates more than 130 buildings that contain equipment for managing voice and data traffic but many are already wired with enough power to run Nvidia’s latest servers, the people said. Nvidia initially floated the idea to Apollo executives, who asked the chipmaker to submit its plans in writing to Brightspeed, according to a third person briefed on the project. Nvidia on Wednesday submitted a proposal and request for additional information, data, and field visits to several sites to Brightspeed, the person said. Nvidia has determined that Brightspeed’s disparate buildings have roughly 1 gigawatt of available power, according to one of the people with knowledge of the effort. That power could potentially run tens of billions of dollars worth of Nvidia Vera Rubin chip systems. Nvidia staff have talked to suppliers about retrofitting some of the Brightspeed buildings with racks of Vera Rubin servers starting in the first quarter of 2027. The plan could also involve installing technology from Groq, the AI chip startup whose technology Nvidia licensed late last year, said the two people with direct knowledge. Upgrades to such facilities, including adding specialized cooling systems for the chips, would likely still require some local government permits or approvals, but fewer than building the facilities from scratch. It isn’t clear who will buy the Nvidia chips for the Brightspeed facilities. But Apollo recently agreed to purchase tens of billions of dollars of Vera Rubin chips, which it will lease to SpaceX, making Apollo one of the world’s biggest buyers of AI server chips . Nvidia representatives have described the proposed Brightspeed data centers as an “inference network,” one of the people said. That term implies the network would power existing AI models rather than help companies develop new models, which typically require a larger, concentrated cluster of chip hardware. Specialized software would help the new owner manage the disparate servers. Customers of these eventual facilities could be cloud providers and AI developers such as SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI. Those companies have been desperate to find additional Nvidia servers to power their businesses amid a server supply crunch and fears of a shortage of power for new facilities. It isn’t clear whether Nvidia or Apollo is talking to those potential customers about the proposal. Anthropic’s Power Hunt Retrofitting old buildings takes advantage of power that would otherwise be underutilized, said Zac Smith, CEO at AI networking startup Datum and longtime cloud executive. But these facilities can also sometimes be more expensive to operate than newer facilities because they might have older, less efficient electrical equipment. Despite such disadvantages, Smith has seen “old telco people” working to retrofit “crappy telco data centers from the ’80s” due to rising demand from cloud firms and AI developers over the past couple of months. Lately, Smith said, companies such as Anthropic have been asking him where they could find pockets of 5 to 10 MW of power capacity in older buildings, he said. Anthropic in particular has told potential investors that a shortage of servers is among the top risks its business faces, and it has accelerated commitments to lease facilities or servers from cloud providers and data center developers to the tune of hundreds of billions of dollars. It isn’t clear exactly how many of the Brightspeed buildings Nvidia wants to retrofit. Many are located in smaller cities such Dothan, Ala., Killeen, Texas, and Mansfield, Ohio. Brightspeed was formed in 2022 after Apollo bought some of telecom firm Lumen Technologies’ local telephone business and broadband assets for $7.5 billion. While the Brightspeed retrofits have taken on added significance since Tuesday’s midterm elections, they also appear to be part of an Nvidia strategy to lock up data center capacity and use up available power for its AI hardware before its rivals do. Nvidia also has made investments in firms that secure power rights and land for new data centers could help Nvidia head off what some data center developers fear is a looming chip overhang in which energy grid delays and local political pushback leave AI hardware sitting idle without electricity.

title: Can Cheaper AI Outrun the Data Center Backlash?
content: After U.S. voters on Tuesday elected officials who are pushing to restrict data center expansion , some tech executives and investors are concerned that new delays in standing up computing capacity will make existing servers for AI more expensive to run. And if computing becomes even pricier, there’s a question of whether declines in the cost of running AI could slow down. So far this year, the cost of running AI has been falling, even as the price of renting servers has risen. For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, released in late September, can perform comparably to a bigger OpenAI flagship model, GPT-6 Astra, when used with a high reasoning setting. Yet the newer model costs about a fifth as much on a per-task basis as the older model, research firm Artificial Analysis said. Anthropic has touted similar efficiencies with its latest models. And that’s happening despite the fact that buying or renting Nvidia hardware has gotten a lot costlier this year. As AI costs become a major concern at enterprises , the price-drop trend will need to persist or else customers might pull back. One senior executive of a private equity firm that owns and develops data centers told me this week that they believe prices of AI models will keep falling due to “token efficiencies”—the ability of AI to do more work with less compute—thanks to both hardware and software advancements. In other words, they said, such efficiencies would help offset constraints on data center expansion. Of course, the executive is heavily incentivized to say such things, given the financial bets their company has already made. On Wednesday, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman said during an event hosted by private equity firm Blackstone that he is optimistic about the company’s data center expansion despite the election results. “We feel like we're in a pretty good spot, and I think others may have some more work to do.” To be sure, Amazon has faced significant local resistance to some of its data center projects, and even had to drop a project in Virginia this year. Garman didn’t comment on whether he expects server rental prices to rise further. But stock investors seemed to think so initially, based on the way they bid up shares of major cloud providers Wednesday while selling off stocks of smaller cloud providers that still need approvals for new facilities. (The major cloud providers pared back some of the gains during a selloff Thursday.) Notably, many facilities that are supposed to come online next year have gotten some or all of the necessary state or local approvals, so the effects of the electoral backlash might have a big impact on facilities aiming to launch in 2028 and beyond. Anthropic’s initial public offering prospectus offers another signal that the price of using its models has room to fall: the company’s gross profit margins have hovered around 85% in the first nine months of the year. (That excludes the cost of developing the models themselves.) So it may have some slack to lower prices if it needs to boost demand. title: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
content:
I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.
The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.
I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.
I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.
Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.
But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.
With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.
But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.
The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.
When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.
Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)
You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.
In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.
The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.
Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.
But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.
Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.

title: Metall gezielt verstärken: Winzige Atomschichten bremsen Verformung
content:
Metall gezielt verstärken: Winzige Atomschichten bremsen Verformung
FAU-Forschende machen Metalllegierungen widerstandsfähiger
Hitze und Dauerbelastung verkürzen die Lebensdauer eines Metallbauteils. Ein internationales Forschungsteam, an dem auch Forschende der Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) mitgewirkt haben, zeigt in einer neuen Studie, wie sich dieser Prozess bremsen lässt. Mit gezielt erzeugten und dünnen Atomschichten machen die Forschende Legierungen widerstandsfähiger. Die Arbeit ist in der Fachzeitschrift Science veröffentlicht worden.
Feste Metalle können unter Hitze und anhaltender Last ihre Form verändern, beispielsweise bei Flugzeugturbinen, in Kraftwerken oder chemischen Anlagen. Dieser Vorgang heißt Kriechen und begrenzt die Lebensdauer eines Bauteils. Ein internationales Forschungsteam unter Beteiligung der FAU und der Ohio State University aus den USA hat einen neuen Ansatz entwickelt mit dem sich Werkstoffe auf atomarer Ebene so gestalten lassen, dass sie dieser Verformung länger standhalten.
An der FAU beteiligt sind Dr. Andreas Bezold, Manuel Köbrich, Jan Vollhüter, Lukas Amon, Prof. Dr. Mathias Göken und Dr. Steffen Neumeier vom Lehrstuhl für Allgemeine Werkstoffeigenschaften. Zusammen mit Nicolas Karpstein und Prof. Dr. Erdmann Spiecker vom Lehrstuhl für Mikro- und Nanostrukturforschung und dem Center for Nanoanalysis and Electron Microscopy untersuchten sie, wie sich widerstandsfähige Strukturen erzeugen lassen.
Winzige Strukturen bremsen Verformungen im Metall
Die Forschenden erzeugten dichte Netzwerke geordneter Schichten, die aus dünnen Atomlagen bestehen. Ähnliche Strukturen können entstehen, wenn sich eine Legierung während ihres Einsatzes verformt. Die Forschenden haben ein Verfahren entwickelt, mit dem sich diese Verformungen bereits vorher herstellen lassen. Ihre festigkeitssteigernde Wirkung kann damit von Anfang an in die Werkstoffentwicklung einbezogen werden.
Anschließend werden die Metalllegierungen mit Wärme behandelt. Hier verteilen sich bereits vorhandene Legierungselemente neu und bilden geordnete Strukturen entlang der atomar dicken Defekte. Dies führt zu einer Änderung der inneren Struktur, die mit einer Steigerung der Festigkeit einhergeht, da die neuen Schichten als Barrieren wirken und damit weitere Verformungen erschweren.
Legierungen im Test: Was Atome über die Festigkeit verraten
Mithilfe von Elektronenmikroskopie und Simulationen konnte das Team zeigen, wie die Anordnung der Atome innerhalb der Schichten zu verbesserten Metall-Eigenschaften beiträgt. Messungen bestätigen diese Ergebnisse: Bei 750 Grad Celsius verformte sich die Superlegierung zudem weniger stark als die Referenzlegierung ohne diese Strukturen. Derartigen Temperaturen müssen die Legierungen zum Beispiel in der Raumfahrt, in Gaskraftwerken oder chemischen Anlagen Stand halten.
Nachhaltigere Werkstoffe
Mögliche Einsatzgebiete für die neuartigen Legierungen sind beispielsweise Turbinen. Langfristig wollen die Forschende untersuchen, ob einfachere Legierungszusammensetzungen vergleichbare mechanische Eigenschaften erreichen. Gelingt das, sind sie deutlich ressourcenschonender.

Wie können kleine Obstbrennereien ihren Energieverbrauch senken? Mit dieser Frage hat sich Ibrahim Abu Mustafa für seine Masterarbeit im Studiengang Process Engineering and Energy Technology (PEET) an der Hochschule Bremerhaven beschäftigt. Seine Ergebnisse zeigen: Die richtige Dämmung würde sich nach wenigen Jahren nicht nur ökologisch, sondern auch wirtschaftlich lohnen.
Der Energieverbrauch einer Obstbrennerei ist im Vergleich zu anderen Getränkeherstellern pro Liter Endprodukt sehr hoch. Dies ist besonders auf die Destillation zurückzuführen, bei der die Obstmaische erhitzt und der entstehende Dampf anschließend wieder verflüssigt wird. Dabei bleibt nicht nur die Abwärme ungenutzt, sondern es wird auch viel Wärme über den Kessel abgegeben. Dass es dafür eine bessere Lösung geben muss, hat sich Masterstudent Ibrahim Abu Mustafa überlegt. Für seine Abschlussarbeit im Studiengang Process Engineering and Energy Technology (PEET) untersuchte er für die Staatliche Lehr- und Versuchsanstalt für Wein- und Obstbau Weinsberg eine 400-Liter-Brennanlage für Obstmaische. Dabei ging es nicht nur um die Frage, ob die Senkung des Energieverbrauchs grundsätzlich möglich ist, sondern auch um die Wirtschaftlichkeit.
Für seine Forschung untersuchte Ibrahim Abu Mustafa zunächst, ob die Wärmeabgabe der Brennanlage durch Dämmung reduziert werden könnte. Hierfür simulierte er am Computer den Wärmeverlust im isolierten und nicht isolierten Zustand. Die Ergebnisse zeigen: Die Dämmung der heißen Kessel- und Anlagenteile kann die Wärmeverluste an den untersuchten Oberflächen um 87 bis 94 Prozent reduzieren. „Bei 134 Brennansätzen pro Jahr ergibt sich für die untersuchte Brennanlage eine Einsparung von rund 823 bis 1.944 kWh Wärme jährlich bei vergleichsweise geringen Investitionskosten. Investiert ein Unternehmen also 1.000 Euro in eine entsprechende Umrüstung der Anlage, würde sich dies auch schnell wirtschaftlich bemerkbar machen. Die geschätzte Amortisationszeit liegt unter den getroffenen Modellannahmen bei einem Strompreis von 0,16 bis 0,20 Euro pro Kilowattstunde zwischen 2,6 und 7,6 Jahren“, so Abu Mustafa. Pauschal auf andere Energiepreise und Wärmeversorgungen lasse sich dies nicht übertragen.
Als weiteren Forschungsschritt widmete sich Ibrahim Abu Mustafa der Abwärme des Kühlwassers, das während der Destillation abgeführt wird. Der Absolvent analysierte zwei Arten von Wärmepumpen, um herauszufinden, ob ihr Einsatz eine sinnvolle Lösung zur Energieeinsparung wäre. Dabei fand er heraus, dass eine Niedertemperatur-Wärmepumpe die Wärme für Warmwasser nutzen und zugleich das Kühlwasser für den nächsten Brennansatz zurückkühlen könnte. In der Simulation lieferte das ausgewählte Szenario 32,09 kW Nutzwärme bei einer Heiz-Leistungszahl von 2,89. Damit ist der ökonomische Nutzen hier nicht so eindeutig. „Die Wirtschaftlichkeit hängt stark davon ab, ob Warmwasser und zurückgekühltes Wasser tatsächlich vor Ort verwendet werden können“, erklärt der Absolvent. Eine Hochtemperatur-Wärmepumpe, die Kühlwasserwärme direkt für den Heizkreis der Brennerei auf über 100 °C anheben soll, sei technisch ebenfalls grundsätzlich machbar. Wegen der hohen Investitionskosten und der geringen jährlichen Betriebszeit von rund 267 Stunden ist sie unter den untersuchten Bedingungen derzeit jedoch wirtschaftlich nicht attraktiv.
Als dritte Möglichkeit könnte auch die Maische mit Rückgewinnungswärme vorgewärmt werden. Die untersuchte Variante mit einem Rohrwärmeübertrager würde Ibrahim Abu Mustafa jedoch nicht empfehlen. „Bei dieser Methode gibt es größere Verschmutzungsrisiken. Außerdem sind die Wärmeübergangswerte eher unsicher und die Wirtschaftlichkeit begrenzt.“ Der Absolvent empfiehlt Brennereien auf Grundlage seiner Ergebnisse zunächst die Dämmung der Anlage, da sich dies auch bei vergleichsweise geringer Betriebszeit schnell wirtschaftlich lohnt. Größere Investitionen, beispielsweise die Installation einer Wärmepumpe, können einen ökologischen Nutzen haben, rentieren sich aber finanziell nur dann, wenn die Anlage viel genutzt wird.
Für die Betreuung und Unterstützung dankt Abu Mustafa Prof. Dr.-Ing. Carsten Fichter und der Hochschule Bremerhaven, Dirk Hofmann von der LVWO Weinsberg sowie dem Anlagenhersteller Arnold Holstein.
Im internationalen, englischsprachigen Masterstudiengang Process Engineering and Energy Technology werden aktuelle Themen der Verfahrenstechnik tiefergehend vermittelt. Dabei geht es um die Untersuchung und Entwicklung technischer Verfahren, die Stoffe nach ihrer Art, ihren Eigenschaften und ihrer Zusammensetzung auf chemischem, physikalischem oder biologischem Wege zu gebrauchsfähigen Zwischen- oder Endprodukten umwandelt. Hierzu gehören auch die Entwicklung, Konstruktion, Fertigung und Wartung der dazu erforderlichen Apparate und Anlagen sowie deren optimaler Betrieb. Die wirtschaftliche und ökologische Nachhaltigkeit sind von entscheidender Bedeutung. So ist die Verfahrenstechnik auch für die Gestaltung und Weiterentwicklung des Klima- und Umweltschutzes sowie der Material- und Energieeffizienz unentbehrlich.

title: Brazil’s state energy planner projects 139 GWh for behind-the-meter BESS by 2036 - Energy Storage
content: The growth of distributed solar generation in Brazil, expected to reach nearly 92 GW of capacity by 2036, is opening space for behind-the-meter (BTM) storage. Brazil’s state-owned energy research agency, Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), estimates that the potential battery market tied to local distributed solar could represent investments of up to BRL 417 billion (USD 75.6 billion) by 2036. The calculation is based on an average projected daily solar generation of 330 GWh in 2036. Of that total, approximately 268 GWh will come from on-site systems, with 139 GWh representing surplus energy injected into the grid. EPE used this exported volume to size the required storage capacity. The investment estimate evaluates battery adoption rates across local solar consumers alongside unit costs ranging between BRL 500/kWh (USD 90/kWh) and BRL 3,000/kWh (USD 532/kWh). Under full adoption (at BRL 3,000/kWh), cumulative investment would reach BRL 417 billion. EPE stresses that this represents market potential rather than an investment forecast, with deployment dependent on cost declines, regulations, and system economics. For Brazil, EPE references turnkey equipment costs of BRL 1,500/kWh ($267/kWh) for commercial and industrial (C&I) systems and BRL 2,750/kWh for residential installations, excluding EPC and grid connection costs. Falling battery prices, wider time-of-use tariffs, and changes to grid injection remuneration under Brazil’s distributed generation law (Law 14,300) will drive storage demand, though economic feasibility remains limited to specific applications. In its 10-year energy plan (PDE 2036), EPE evaluated three BTM use cases: increasing self-consumption in microgeneration, load management for mid-voltage C&I consumers on green tariffs, and time-of-use tariff arbitrage for low-voltage consumers. For self-consumption, batteries store excess solar for later use, cutting grid injection. However, storage currently lengthens payback periods compared to standalone PV. Phased reductions in export credits under Law 14,300 encourage self-consumption, but falling acquisition costs remain the critical factor to bring payback times into competitive territory. For mid-voltage C&I consumers, batteries charge off-peak and discharge during expensive peak hours. EPE identified this application as offering the highest economic potential. In the regulated captive market, systems yield positive net present value (NPV) across all evaluated cost bands. In the free market, storage remains viable up to roughly BRL 1,000/kWh with grid tariff discounts, and up to BRL 1,500/kWh without discounts due to wider peak/off-peak spreads. For low-voltage residential and commercial consumers, tariff arbitrage yields much narrower margins. Positive NPV appears almost exclusively when battery costs fall below BRL 500/kWh, with results turning predominantly negative above BRL 1,000/kWh. Despite these hurdles, EPE expects solar-plus-storage to carve out specific niches over the coming decade, particularly among consumers prioritizing power resilience. title: China connected 60 MW/600 MWh liquid-air storage facility in Qinghai - Energy Storage
content: A 60 MW/600 MWh LAES demonstration project in Qinghai province, northwest China, was connected to the grid and began generating electricity on October 30, marking a significant step toward the commercial deployment of large-scale cryogenic energy storage. Located in Golmud, Haixi Mongolian and Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, the facility was developed by state-owned China Green Development Investment Group (CGDG) in cooperation with the Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). The developer describes the project as the world’s largest grid-connected liquid-air energy storage facility by both rated power and energy capacity. Construction began in July 2023. The project was selected for China’s national new-type energy storage demonstration program and included in the National Energy Administration’s list of major first-of-a-kind energy technologies and equipment. With a rated output of 60 MW and a storage capacity of 600 MWh, the facility is designed to deliver electricity continuously for 10 hours. According to CGDG, it could accommodate approximately 600 MWh of surplus renewable electricity daily and supply an estimated 180 GWh to the grid annually, equivalent to the electricity consumption of around 30,000 households. The system uses ambient air as its working fluid, avoiding the need for electrochemical batteries or underground storage caverns. When charging, surplus electricity drives a three-stage centrifugal compressor, pressurizing purified air to approximately 7 MPa. Heat generated during compression is recovered and stored as hot water at temperatures reaching 195 C. The compressed air then passes through a multistage cooling process before being liquefied at approximately -194 C and stored in insulated cryogenic tanks at near-atmospheric pressure. During discharge, the liquid air is pressurized, reheated and vaporized. The expanding gas drives turbines connected to generators, while cold energy recovered during vaporization is stored for reuse in subsequent charging cycles. The project incorporates several domestically developed technologies, including large centrifugal compressors, liquid expanders, cryogenic heat exchangers and integrated control systems. CGDG said all major equipment was manufactured domestically, achieving a 100% localization rate. The technology was developed through collaboration between CGDG and CAS researchers, who previously demonstrated liquid-air energy storage at the 100-kW scale. Engineering design was undertaken by Hualu Engineering & Technology, with China National Chemical Engineering Third Construction participating in construction. Unlike many compressed-air energy storage configurations that require suitable geological formations, liquid-air storage uses insulated tanks, allowing greater flexibility in site selection. The rotating machinery can also provide inertial support to the power grid, according to the project developer. The facility is located in Qinghai’s renewable-rich Qaidam Basin, where long-duration storage could help shift surplus solar and wind generation to periods of higher electricity demand. China is pursuing multiple long-duration energy storage technologies alongside its dominant lithium-ion battery industry. Compressed-air systems, vanadium redox flow batteries, sodium-ion batteries and thermal storage are being developed for different operating durations and grid applications. The latest Golmud project provides a large-scale engineering demonstration for liquid-air storage. title: El Pelícano raises $129.58 million for solar-plus-storage in Chile - Energy Storage
content: El Pelícano Solar Co. SpA has secured $129.58 million through a secured bond issuance to refinance existing debt and, among other purposes, finance the development and construction of a BESS alongside its 110 MW solar plant in Chile. The transaction closed in early October, according to law firm Clifford Chance, which advised the company. The financing was structured in two stages. The first was a bridge loan signed on July 1, 2026, with BNP Paribas acting as lender and administrative agent and BNP Paribas Securities Corp. as lead arranger. The loan was subsequently refinanced through a private placement of senior secured notes. The notes, issued by El Pelícano Solar Co., carry an interest rate of 7.578% and mature on Dec. 31, 2044. The placement was made to private investors under the registration exemption provided by Section 4(a)(2) of the US Securities Act. BNP Paribas acted as placement agent. According to Clifford Chance, proceeds from the transaction will be used, among other purposes, to develop and build an 82 MW battery energy storage system with four hours of duration. However, Chile’s National Energy Commission (CNE) lists the El Pelícano BESS project with a net power capacity of 75 MW and an energy storage capacity of 300 MWh. The two sources therefore report different power capacities, although both indicate four hours of storage. The project is listed as under construction in records from Chile’s Ministry of Energy. Its May 2026 report gives an estimated investment of $61 million and a planned interconnection date of February 2027 to the National Electric System (SEN). The installation will use lithium-ion batteries and connect to the 23 kV El Pelícano substation. The estimated investment in the BESS is separate from the total financing amount, which also covers debt refinancing. The El Pelícano solar plant began commercial operations in November 2017. Developed by SunPower, it was subsequently acquired by Actis. The facility supplies electricity to the Santiago Metro under a 15-year power purchase agreement (PPA). As reported by pv magazine in December 2016, the plant was expected to supply around 300 GWh annually, equivalent to 42% of the transport network’s electricity consumption. The project has 254,880 solar modules spread across approximately 186 hectares. The addition of battery storage will allow some solar generation to be shifted to periods of higher demand and help use electricity that could otherwise be subject to grid-injection restrictions caused by network congestion. According to Clifford Chance and White & Case, which advised the parties to the transaction, the issuance represents the first capital markets financing in Chile for a battery storage project associated with a single asset. title: Spanish companies plan district heating networks powered by data center waste heat - pv magazine Global
content:
Spanish companies Ignis and Rebi have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore the development of district heating networks using waste heat from data centers. The aim is to recover thermal energy generated during data center operations and use it to supply heat to residential buildings, commercial facilities and industrial processes.
The collaboration will focus on data center projects that Ignis is developing in partnership with specialized operators. The two companies will assess solutions to integrate data center cooling systems with waste heat recovery and distribution technologies.
The feasibility of each project will depend on nearby heat demand and the technical conditions required to connect the data center to a district heating network. Such integration could replace some conventional heat generation, reducing fuel consumption for heating and industrial processes.
Rebi will contribute its expertise in designing, building and operating district heating networks, while Ignis will assess how these solutions could be integrated into its data center project portfolio and energy management operations.
Rebi currently operates six district heating networks in Spain and develops heating solutions for the residential, commercial and industrial sectors. Its technology portfolio includes biomass, waste heat recovery, heat pumps, hybrid solar systems and thermal energy storage.
Ignis develops and manages energy projects for large-scale consumers and emerging electricity demand, including data centers. The company has more than 1 GW of generation capacity in operation or under construction and manages approximately 10 GW of assets, including its own and third-party facilities.

title: Optimal solar module tilt angle for hail protection is site-specific, researchers find - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers in Iran have developed a computational model to predict hailstone trajectories and impact severity on PV modules under different wind conditions and panel tilt angles. The model accounts for wind speed, wind direction, and hailstone aerodynamics to assess potential mechanical damage to solar panels.
“We considered the combined effects of wind speed, wind direction, hailstone aerodynamic behavior, and photovoltaic panel tilt angle,” corresponding author Armin Hasanpour told
pv magazine
. “The trajectories were calculated by considering gravitational and aerodynamic forces and solving the governing equations using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method.”
Hasanpour said the team aimed to develop mathematical relationships and numerical tools to predict potential hailstorm damage.
“Such quantitative approaches could eventually contribute to photovoltaic hail-risk databases used by insurance companies, support policymakers in assessing climate-related risks, and help designers determine more appropriate panel tilt angles based on local meteorological conditions,” he said.
The researchers used a 3 MW solar project in Takestan, Iran, as a case study, drawing on regional weather records from 2004 to 2024 to characterize local conditions. They developed a numerical model to simulate spherical hailstones with diameters ranging from 1 cm to 10 cm under wind speeds of 1 m/s to 50 m/s, assuming constant air and ice densities and an initial release height of 2,000 m.
The model incorporated gravitational forces and aerodynamic drag, with the governing equations solved using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method. The researchers compared simulations using constant drag coefficients with those using Reynolds-number-dependent coefficients.
They projected the calculated impact velocities onto the direction normal to the panel surface to determine the perpendicular component of kinetic energy. The site-specific analysis compared panel tilt angles of 25° and 30° under four wind scenarios: 22.8 m/s from 350°, and 24 m/s from 200°, 350°, and 360°.
The researchers also developed a conceptual damage model using an assumed critical energy threshold of 2 J to classify impacts and illustrate potential cracking and indentation. They validated the simulation results against an angle-adjusted theoretical impact-energy calculation.
“One of the most interesting findings was the significant influence of wind direction on hailstone impact conditions,” Hasanpour said. “Wind speed alone cannot adequately describe the impact behavior; the interaction between wind direction, wind speed, and panel orientation can substantially change the angle and energy distribution of an impact.”
Hasanpour said another important finding concerned the drag coefficient. For relatively large hailstones, particularly those with diameters of 8 cm or more, assuming a constant drag coefficient could result in deviations of up to approximately 14% compared with calculations using a variable drag coefficient.
“This demonstrates why aerodynamic assumptions should be carefully considered when developing predictive models,” he said.
“We also found that changing the photovoltaic panel tilt angle from 25° to 30° alters the impact characteristics and the component of kinetic energy acting perpendicular to the panel surface,” Hasanpour concluded. “This suggests that panel orientation should not be selected based on energy production alone; local hailstorm conditions and potential damage risks should also be considered.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
Numerical modeling and analysis of weather conditions effects on hail impact severity and damage to photovoltaic panels
,” which was recently published in
Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments
. The research team included scientists from Iran’s Shahrood University of Technology, Radsun Energy Pars, and Asoo Vision Pardaz.

title: Laser-based recycling method enables over 95% selective silver recovery from end-of-life solar panels - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers led by the
University of Glasgow
in Scotland have developed a laser-induced delamination method for recycling aged crystalline silicon solar modules. The process separates the ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulant from the silicon cells, producing cleaner material streams for the subsequent selective recovery of silver and aluminum.
“End-of-life crystalline-silicon photovoltaic modules remain difficult to recycle because EVA adheres strongly to cell interfaces, and dominant routes rely on shredding or bulk thermal treatment, generating mixed fractions,” the researchers said. “This study demonstrates that laser-induced delamination provides a selective, dry pathway for removing EVA from aged c-Si PV laminates by targeting the EVA–Si interface, thus reducing the intermixing of materials.”
The researchers combined hot-knife glass removal with laser-induced delamination to separate aged PV laminates into three material streams: largely intact EVA films containing trace metal residues, isolated busbars, and silicon-rich cell powder. They tested two types of modules aged approximately 10 to 13 years, using a 1,064 nm fiber laser to target the EVA-silicon interface.
The experiments involved laser powers ranging from 9 W to 27 W at pulse frequencies of 30 kHz, 40 kHz, and 50 kHz on 20 mm × 20 mm samples, with additional tests conducted on larger specimens.
The researchers subjected the resulting powder to sequential leaching with 1 M sodium hydroxide to remove aluminum, followed by an iron(III) chloride-choline chloride brine to extract silver, leaving crystalline silicon. They compared the extraction results with a nitric acid benchmark and assessed the separation process using sample weighing, microscopy, spectroscopy, thermal analysis, and X-ray diffraction.
The tests showed that EVA separation began at approximately 12 W to 14 W, with nearly complete separation achieved at around 18 W to 20 W and higher. The process produced largely intact EVA films, isolated busbars, and silicon-rich powder with negligible polymer contamination.
Sequential leaching achieved silver extraction selectivity of more than 95% for both module types, exceeding 99% in one case. Extracted silver accounted for 1.08% to 1.38% of the powder mass, while aluminum removal ranged from 7.79% to 8.54%.
X-ray diffraction confirmed that crystalline silicon remained after treatment, while diffraction peaks associated with silver and aluminum disappeared. Small amounts of metal residues remained in the EVA, particularly around busbar contact regions, suggesting potential for further recovery.
“To the best of our knowledge, this is the most selective silver extraction reported for aged panels,” the researchers concluded. “Because the laser targets only the EVA–silicon interface, not the bulk laminate, the hot-knife plus laser route should need less energy than pyrolysis or thermo-solvent treatment, lowering process intensity while improving chemical tractability for selective metals recovery.”
The researchers presented their findings in “
Laser-induced delamination of aged silicon photovoltaic modules to achieve >95% selective silver recovery
,” which was recently published in Communications Materials. The research team included scientists from Saudi Arabia’s
Princess Nourah bint Abdulrahman University
and Germany’s
Fraunhofer Center for Silicon Photovoltaics (CSP)

title: Phnix unveils all-in-one propane heat pump with 6 kW heating capacity - pv magazine Global
content:
Chinese heat pump manufacturer
has launched GreenTherm One, an all-in-one air-to-water heat pump designed for residential heating, cooling and domestic hot water applications.
The company said the new system integrates a thermal storage tank and key hydraulic components into a single outdoor unit, eliminating the need for a separate indoor hot water cylinder. According to Phnix, the plug-and-play design enables installation in as little as one hour, provided the site has been prepared beforehand.
The heat pump uses propane (R290) as a refrigerant, with a charge of 0.35 kg. It has a nominal heating capacity of 6 kW and a modulation range of 1.5 kW to 7.5 kW at an outdoor temperature of 7 C and a water outlet temperature of 35 C. At a water outlet temperature of 55 C, the heating capacity ranges from 1.4 kW to 7.0 kW.
The manufacturer reports an seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) of 5.1 at 35 C and 3.85 at 55 C. The unit can reportedly deliver outlet water temperatures of up to 75 C and operates at outdoor temperatures ranging from -25 C to 45 C.
In cooling mode, the heat pump delivers between 1.36 kW and 7.5 kW at an outdoor air temperature of 35 C and a chilled-water outlet temperature of 18C (A35/W18). It uses a single-phase 220 V to 240 V power supply at 50 Hz.
The heat pump measures 750 mm × 580 mm × 1,950 mm and weighs 185 kg. It has a rated water flow of 0.86 m3/h, a sound pressure level of 38 dB(A) at a distance of 1 meter and a sound power level of 55 dB(A), measured according to EN 12102.
The integrated thermal storage tank stores heating energy rather than potable water. Domestic hot water is produced on demand as fresh water passes through the system, which the manufacturer says reduces the risk of bacterial growth associated with stored drinking water.
The unit also incorporates a circulation pump, a microbubble air separator and a safety valve. An optional refrigerant leakage detector is also available.
Phnix said the system features inverter-based controls that adjust compressor operation according to heating demand. Its smart grid functionality enables operation to be scheduled according to electricity tariffs, while an optional iDrive Box allows the heat pump to coordinate operation with available rooftop PV generation to increase solar self-consumption.
The company said GreenTherm One can also be integrated with existing boilers for hybrid heating applications, making it suitable for both new residential buildings and renovation projects.
Phnix has not disclosed the integrated thermal storage capacity, domestic hot water delivery rate or pricing and commercial availability details.

title: China wafer prices steady on firm polysilicon amid weak fundamentals - pv magazine Global
content:
Free-On-Board (FOB) China prices for n-type M10 and 210R wafers remained stable week on week at $0.146/pc and $0.153/pc, respectively, according to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Nov. 3.
According to market participants, wafer price stability has been supported primarily by firm polysilicon prices. In addition, improving supply-demand dynamics in the solar cell segment, underpinned by overseas demand and domestic end-market installation activity, have provided further support for wafer prices.
Industry sources said that major wafer manufacturers have largely maintained the reduced operating rates implemented in October, with little change since the beginning of November. Leading wafer producers continue to operate at approximately 45%-50% capacity, while specialized manufacturers are maintaining operating rates above 60%.
However, these production adjustments have yet to translate into a meaningful improvement in overall market fundamentals, with oversupply and elevated inventory levels continuing to weigh on the wafer market. Market participants estimated that wafer inventories currently stand at the upper end of the 20-30 GW range. With these structural imbalances yet to ease, sources said the price outlook remains subdued, particularly if downstream demand weakens further.
Another industry source shared a similar assessment, describing the wafer market as fundamentally weak and noting that its pricing outlook remains highly dependent on supply-demand dynamics and price trends across both upstream and downstream segments. The source added that once polysilicon prices come under downward pressure, wafer prices are unlikely to remain insulated from the impact.
A major wafer manufacturer said that transaction volumes remain relatively modest, with customers continuing to adopt a cautious procurement approach. Buyers are closely monitoring potential downstream price declines in December, particularly amid expectations of a seasonal slowdown in demand. Nevertheless, the manufacturer said it currently has little incentive to lower prices, as further price reductions alone are unlikely to stimulate additional purchasing beyond customers’ immediate procurement needs.
Meanwhile, another trade participant noted that demand for large-format n-type G12 wafers is also expected to gradually soften as November progresses, after strong demand from China’s ground-mounted solar projects supported upward price momentum over the previous two months. The source said wafer prices may decline in stages across different sizes, with smaller-format wafers likely to come under downward pressure first, followed gradually by larger-format products.
Upstream, the China Mono Premium, the OPIS assessment for mono-grade polysilicon used in n-type ingot production, was unchanged week on week at CNY 38.786 ($5.81)/kg.
According to market sources, the underlying fundamentals of the Chinese polysilicon market remain weak. Inventory levels exceeding 500,000 metric tons, monthly production continuing to outpace demand, and sluggish downstream consumption continue to weigh on market sentiment.
Nevertheless, one encouraging development is the anticipated impact of production cuts initiated by polysilicon manufacturers in October, with the resulting reduction in supply likely to become more evident from November onwards.
Despite the anticipated improvement in supply-demand dynamics, some trade participants have observed signs of further price declines during ongoing negotiations between buyers and sellers, largely attributed to mounting financial pressure on suppliers and the approaching seasonal slowdown in end-user demand.
One trade participant said the apparent stability in polysilicon prices is somewhat misleading, as it is being maintained largely through an industry self-discipline agreement that currently carries no penalties for non-compliance. For companies facing financial difficulties, breaking ranks by resuming production or offering lower prices ahead of others may therefore appear to be the most viable way out, the participant added.
Taking a longer view, an upstream industry source said the agreement alone is insufficient to establish a sustainable price floor, cautioning that a meaningful recovery in the PV sector remains a long way off. Such a recovery will require time and progress across several fronts, including the gradual reduction of polysilicon inventories, sustained production rationalization, improved corporate profitability, technological upgrades and production-line optimization, and further consolidation through mergers and acquisitions, the source added.
OPIS, a Dow Jones company, provides energy prices, news, data, and analysis on gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, LPG/NGL, coal, metals, and chemicals, as well as renewable fuels and environmental commodities. It acquired pricing data assets from Singapore Solar Exchange in 2022 and now publishes the

title: EcoFlow launches two new series of portable power stations - pv magazine Global
content:
EcoFlow, known for portable power solutions and an expanding residential focus, has launched two new series of portable power stations.
The Delta Gen4 and River Gen4 are both evolutions of well-known portable and backup power offerings, with EcoFlow seeking to shake up its design language, package into smaller volumes with weight reductions, and reduce power consumption.
Delta Gen4 series
The new models in the Delta Gen 4 series are the Delta 3800 Gen4 and 3000 Gen4, with the model numbers correlating to storage capacity: the 3800 Gen4 offers 3763 Wh (3.7 kWh), and the 3000 Gen4 offers 3072 Wh.
Both new Delta Gen4 models deliver 3.6 kW rated AC output and 7.2 kW surge power for heavy startup inrush currents. The Delta 3000 Gen4 has four charging methods, including AC, generator, solar PV, and alternator car charger, while Delta 3800 has six, adding solar plus alternator charging and solar plus generator.
In terms of weight, the 3800 Gen4 weighs 67.5 lbs or 30.6 kg, while DELTA 3000 Gen4 weighs 57.3 lbs or almost 26 kg.
Image: Flickr/
grassrootsgroundswell
EcoFlow Delta Gen4 weight and features
EcoFlow claims both are the smallest and lightest portable power stations in their classes by capacity per pound.
This is slightly apples and oranges: based solely on spec sheets, the Anker S5000, with 5,024 Wh at 97 lbs, offers 51.8 Wh per pound, compared with EcoFlow’s best density at 3763 Wh at 67.5 lbs, or 55.7 Wh per pound.
However the
ESS News
deep dive review of the S5000
did commend the unit for coming with wheels, along with a telescopic handle for portability. The EcoFlow Delta Gen4 series doesn’t offer wheels, just handles, which keeps packaging tighter and overall lighter, but may need a separate trolley to be truly portable.
EcoFlow says both models reduce their own power consumption by up to 70%, drawing just 14W with AC on (no load) and 3W in standby, compared with quoted industry averages of over 20W and 10W.
Adding intelligence to the mix, a mode of operation called Fridge Runtime Boost “reduces unnecessary energy use between refrigerator cooling cycles,” helping “keep food cold for 2–3 days during an outage”.
A new Emergency Power Mode is also available, which forces a power station to reserve capacity for emergency DC power for supplying devices through longer outages, such as phones, even as the battery level reaches 0% on the display.
For added outage preparedness, Storm Guard Mode 2.0 integrates professional weather
data from the National Weather Service in the U.S. to help users prepare their power stations ahead of severe weather and potential outages.
In UPS mode, a 10ms UPS switchover keeps connected electronics running through interruptions.
River Gen4 Series
On the smaller-size front is the new River Gen4 series, featuring the River 260 Gen4 and River 520 Gen4. Again, the model numbers align with capacity, with the 260 Gen4 packing 256Wh of capacity and 300 W power output in a more compact design that’s just over 6 lb, while the River 520 Gen4 packs 512Wh of capacity and 500 W output into a 10 lb design. Both feature removable carrying straps for easy portability.
The shift to reducing standby power is also evident here, with power draw at 6.6 W with AC on and 1 W in standby. Both models support four charging methods (AC, USB-C, solar and alternator), and include multiple AC and USB ports, including 140W bidirectional USB-C.
The River Gen4 series also offers Emergency Power Mode and UPS functionality.
Delta Gen4 and River Gen4 pricing and availability
EcoFlow says the Delta Gen4 is now available on the EcoFlow website with early-bird pricing at $1,299 for DELTA 3000 Gen4 and $1,699 for DELTA 3800 Gen4.
The River Gen4 series will be available for pre-sale beginning November 24.
Availability in other regions is dependent on EcoFlow’s rollout.
EcoFlow in Japan actually launched the Delta and River Gen4 series earlier than the US, where they have been available since October 30th.
In Germany, the River 260 Gen4 is available from November 16th.
For the Delta Gen4, a spokesperson responded to a question from
ESS News
, saying that EcoFlow is still confirming dates for European availability
EcoFlow Black Friday deals
EcoFlow also announced its Black Friday sales began on November 2 and will run through December 7 in the US.
In Germany, EcoFlow also announced Black Friday deals on the Stream series and Delta 3 series starting November 10 and November 13th respectively.
In Australia, a “sneak peek” early launch of Black Friday deals also began.
